speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DAIRY POLICY COMMENCING APRIL 1, 1973
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the House of the dairy policy for the year starting April 1.
The government has concluded that in order to ensure an adequate supply of dairy products for Canadian consumers, it is necessary to take steps to help dairy farmers meet the rising cost of production with which they have been faced, costs that have escalated rapidly in recent months due partly to worldwide shortages of feed grains and protein supplements.
It will be appreciated that in deciding on measures to that end, consideration had to be given to the present concern over food prices. The decision, therefore, is that only part of the increase will come from the market, and part from subsidy payments to producers for manufacturing milk and cream.
The Canadian Dairy Commission has been authorized to set its support price on butter, effective April 1, at 71 cents per pound; the level in the year just ending has been 68 cents. This is an increase of just over 4 per cent. It may be noted, however, that the new price is only 9 per cent higher than in 1967, which was the first year of the commission's operations. Over that six year period this works out to an average annual increase of slightly over 1 per cent.
The new support price on skim milk powder will be 35 cents per pound. The present price is 29 cents.
The support price for Cheddar cheese, affective April 1 will be 60 cents per pound, up six cents from the level in effect in 1972-73 but below current market price.
The rate of direct subsidy to producers is to be increased by 20 cents per hundred pounds of milk, or 5.71 cents per pound butterfat. The total new rate will then be $1.45 per hundred pounds of milk, or 41.42 cents per
pound of butterfat. The new rate will apply to quota deliveries of manufacturing milk and cream on and after April 1. It is considered that the changed relationship between the domestic and the international price for skim milk powder will necessitate the Canadian Dairy Commission increasing the rate of producer levy to 30 cents per hundred pounds of milk.
I should point out that it is not possible to state precisely the impact of these changes in terms of increased returns to producers, since the federal government does not set market prices paid to producers. Any such authority rests with provincial agencies. However, a straight calculation, if all the benefits were reflected in producer prices, equates with approximately 60 cents per hundred pounds of milk.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DAIRY POLICY COMMENCING APRIL 1, 1973
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I should like to thank the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) for his courtesy in making this statement available to our party in ample time to be aware of the announcement to the House today.
I should like to begin by saying that I am rather shocked at the statement that has been made today. This statement represents the government's reaction to the chaotic economic state of the dairy industry in Canada today. It represents for one year all the concentrated action of this government on behalf of an industry which, for many months and in many ways, has made direct representations to this government. It represents the government's action on behalf of an industry which has found that in the past year it has been unable to fully meet the dairy requirements of this country. It is all very well for the minister to intimate that poor weather conditions made it impossible for us to meet our commitments. However, this excuse does not hold true because this is not the first time in the last three or four years that the dairy industry has been put into a position where it could not meet our domestic requirements. What this policy represents to the dairy industry is the very minimum that the government considers necessary for sustaining this industry in Canada in a viable state.
It is unfortunate that the minister, who has a farm background, and this new government did not see fit at this time to change policy to such an extent that we might have had some indication of a long term policy for keeping this industry stable in the country.

March 29, 1973
The Dairy Policy
when other countries appreciate the value of our cattle and offer fabulous sums to the producers of this country for cattle which are exported, at a time when this government is encouraging the importation of dairy products into this country and at the very time when we need stability as never before if we are to combat high food prices, this is the policy the government has adopted in order to sustain and keep this industry viable.
I should like to say one thing in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, and it is this: The government and the Department of Agriculture cannot solve any of the problems in agriculture today if all they are concerned about is providing from day to day the most minimal assistance to this industry. It must operate on a basis of profit if we are to have the type of industry that Canadians can be proud of and one that will produce the food Canadians need.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DAIRY POLICY COMMENCING APRIL 1, 1973
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I asked the minister some questions about dairy policy and cheese. He said he had been speaking with people in the dairy industry and that he would have answers. At any rate, this is a pretty weak answer, and I do not think it represents the comprehensive approach we need to take at this time to the dairy industry of Canada.
Yesterday, men representing a cheese factory in Ontario came to meet with my party. They asked if there was not some way in which they could get enough raw milk to keep that cheese factory going. At the same time the authorities in Saskatchewan are trying to persuade people to go into cheese production, after having driven farmers out of butter production three or four years ago. The statement that has been made to us in no way answers some of the real needs of the industry.
The minister did not tell us that we will need to import over 20 million pounds of butter this year; yet here we are, one of the largest agricultural producing countries in the world and we cannot produce enough butter for our own needs. We have been driving smaller farmers and smaller cheese factories out of production. Actually, the government gives them a bonus if they get out of production. Yet these same farmers and same cheese producers are begging to be allowed to produce more of their product, because they say there is an unlimited market, as far as they are concerned, for good Canadian Cheddar cheese.
The small amount of money that is being put up will help. I wonder if the minister thinks it will answer the purposes of those people whom he met in Smiths Falls. They told him they could not afford to hire enough help to effectively operate their dairy farm. I wonder if the minister thinks that the 1 per cent increase he is granting for this year under this policy, and about which he probably boasts, is going to meet the increased costs the dairy farmers in Canada have to absorb. I hope the minister has better plans and a better program for the dairy farmers of this country than that set out in the statement which he has made to this House today.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to make a suggestion which I hope will cover all departments. Since the offices of the members are not

all located in the same building, when a minister is to make a statement, would it be possible to send a copy to each member of the standing committee concerned, which in my opinion would be very helpful to all? I am not blaming the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) because he surely sent a copy of his statement to our leader, but since our offices are in another building we can barely examine the statements before the opening of a sitting.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that we were eagerly waiting the statement of the Minister of Agriculture disclosing the dairy policy of the government for the year beginning on April 1, 1973.
In the statement that has just been made, I wish indeed that the minister had considered the increase in production costs which has occurred, particularly since the fall of 1972, because dairy producers have had to purchase more feed because of the poor crops in 1972.
Considering that production costs have gone up in the fall of 1972, I would have hoped at least that the increase announced today would be retroactive to November 1972. Would it be worse for farm workers to to benefit retroactively from the effects of one decision or the other than for workers of other industries who benefit from the retroactive effects of collective bargaining?
The long term objective of the Canadian Dairy Commission is to guarantee to dairy producers an income and stability comparable with those of other sectors of the economy, otherwise an industry could not today remain prosperous for long. The commission is also expected to maintain and boost the consumption of milk and dairy products in Canada.
If these two aims are not reached, the quality of food will be noticeably reduced, and with it the quality of life of our urban and rural populations.
It is a fact that the returns that industrial milk and cream producers are getting for their products have become totally unacceptable and must be raised further; representations to that effect have been made by the industrial milk producers, the Federation of Industrial Milk Producers and also the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
I do think that all the minister's meetings with these organizations have been profitable, but more notice should have been taken of the representations that have been made.
Not so long ago, Mr. Speaker, the returns from the market, combined with direct subsidies to industrial milk producers, had finally, after years of insufficient income, reached a level sufficiently in excess of the overheads to allow something like a fair degree of remuneration. But in the last few months' costs have risen sharply all along the line, especially those of feed grain and mill feed.
Since November, the price of dairy mill feed with 16 per cent protein content has gone up from $70 to $100 a ton. That is why I claim that the increased subsidy rate should be made retroactive to November 1972, so as to guarantee industrial milk producers a reasonable income for their winter production. It is also urgent to solve the problem of feed grain without delay.
March 29, 1973

We sometimes hear people saying that the industrial milk producers are asking too much, or that they are incompetent and poor administrators, and that current prices should allow them ample returns. That is what some people say.
Strange, Mr. Speaker, that those people who act as experts in the forum of the dairy industry should not deal themselves in that production to give the example of their knowledge and the secret of their success. That would really help milk producers.
In conclusion, I say that I am always astounded to hear the comments when an increase in the cost of living is announced. It is always the same old story: if the cost of living goes up, the farmers are to blame, which is contrary to the facts. I therefore suggest that, to satisfy both producers and consumers, a discount should be decreed on the cost of dairy products, discount that would lower consumer prices and check rising prices. That discount would be made up to the producers by the Agricultural Stabilization Board through new credits made available to it by the Bank of Canada. In that way, both consumers and producers would be happy.
It is urgent that farm producers get a higher net income if they are to stay in business and if we want to encourage the young to go into farming.
In La Terre de Chez Nous dated March 21, Mr. Speaker, at least 50 auction sales were advertised, of which most were dairy operations.
The danger is serious. Unless more people devote their time to agriculture, there will be a shortage of Canadian farm produce. They will then have to be imported, at higher costs, and when a country depends on others for its food, it loses its freedom and security.
Those, then, Mr. Speaker, were the suggestions and remarks I wanted to make in all honesty, as a conclusion to my criticism. I hope the minister will keep that in mind and that he will recommend to the cabinet that they be adopted as soon as possible.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: TABLING OF MOTIONS RELATING TO INCOME TAX, SALES TAX AND CUSTOMS TARIFF-DESIGNATION OF ORDER OF THE DAY FOR DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to table several notices of ways and means motions relating to income taxes, sales taxes arid the customs tariff, pursuant to Standing Order 60, paragraph one. In part they supersede notices tabled at the time of my February budget, and in part they reintroduce proposals which I made to this House in my budget of May 1972. In view of the interest and importance we all attach to these matters, I should like to take a moment to outline the contents of the notices to the House.
Members of the House will be aware of the main income tax measures proposed in the two budgets. All are vitally important to Canadians, but enactment of some is more urgent than others. In particular, I am referring to the measures which affect taxpayers in the taxation year 1972. Many taxpayers who have filed, or will be filing by April 30, 1972 tax returns are affected by measures announced in the May and the February budgets. In respect of these taxpayers, final assessments cannot be made and refunds, where they are due to taxpayers, cannot be paid until parliament has acted. The highest priority therefore attaches to all the measures which affect the 1972 taxation year.
For this reason, the notices of ways and means motions I am tabling today affecting income taxes, and the bill which will be based upon them, will deal with the measures of the May and February budgets affecting taxpayers for the year 1972. These proposals include the increase in the old age exemption, the new education expense deduction, the new provisions in respect of medical expenses, the tax free transfer of the family farm to children upon death, the elimination of the ineligible investment test for small businesses and a number of items arising out of tax reform.
I also wish to table two further notices of ways and means motions covering the sales tax and custom tariff changes proposed in the May budget. In the main, the measures announced in the budget of last May took effect in 1972 and, therefore, should also be given prior consideration.
I would urge the House to deal expeditiously with these 1972 tax measures.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) who has just supplied us with the French text of his statement.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to repeat the remarks of the two previous speakers, which were to the point, but certain words cannot go without some comment from our corner of the House, specifically on page 2 of the minister's statement, from which I quote:
I would urge the House to deal expeditiously with these 1972 tax measures.
Dealing expeditiously with 1972 tax measures, when we are in April 1973 is a mockery of the taxpayers, specially those, thousands of them, who have already paid out fees to accountants for preparation of their tax returns on time, because they do not always leave them to the last minute. The minister indeed recognizes this in his statement, saying on page 1, and I quote:
Many taxpayers who have filed, or will be filing by April 30, their 1972 tax returns are affected by measures announced in the May and the February budgets. In respect of these taxpayers, final assessment cannot be made and refunds, where they are due to taxpayers, cannot be paid until parliament has acted.
Now, Mr. Speaker, those measures are not yet known to us and we have before us today clear proof that some taxpayers, or most of them, will have to make out new returns, as a result of the new measures. They will have to pay out professional fees again for drawing up this second return, all because of the Minister of Finance's lack of foresight in not announcing at least a month or 60 days in advance the measures he will be introducing next Tuesday.
That shows, Mr. Speaker, that once again politics are being practiced to the detriment of low-income Canadian taxpayers, and also that the present parliament-and because of parliament all of us-do not know where it is headed for in the fiscal field.
The Minister of Finance might announce other measures tomorrow. When will it end? He may announce new measures to amend tax regulations or the May or February budgets.
It is ridiculous, Mr. Speaker, to see that the Minister of Finance who, I admit, is a nice fellow, since he has taken part in some very popular contests in Quebec, does not make more "attractive" his tax measures and recommendations, which will clearly not be passed next Tuesday. These new measures will force thousands of taxpayers to revise their tax returns, taxpayers who have already been puzzling over them for months, only to have to start afresh in the light of the minister's statement.
I consider that the Minister of Finance ought to make more "attractive" and clearer, not only his statements and the programs on which he works, but also his financial and fiscal policy.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity to seek unanimous consent of the House to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. My motion concerns every livestock producer in Canada in that hog prices in the United States have dropped $13 in the last two weeks, which is a 24 per cent drop, and live cattle prices have dropped $3 and are still dropping. Canadian hog prices have now dropped 20 per cent in two weeks, no doubt triggered by the Japanese withdrawal from our Canadian pork market.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO JUNE 30, 1976
speechtext:
that Bill C-130, to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill the House is now being asked to consider provides for the extension of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act for a further period of three years, that is to say, to June 30, 1976. In this period there will be no change in the method of calculating the amount of assistance that will be payable to the operators of gold mines. This is pursuant to an announcement I made on June 21, 1972, indicating the intention of the government to extend the act in order to ensure the stability of the gold mines and the future of the communities dependent upon them.
The prospects of those gold mines which have survived the steady decline in the industry-these hon. members will find in the report on the administration of the act which I tabled in the House at the beginning of the session-are now greatly improved because of the current level of the open market price for gold. Should the current level be maintained in the open market for gold and operators continue to sell their gold on the open market, then the assitance that is available under the act will not be required. With an open market price above $48 per ounce-I shall give a review of the prices to the House in a moment-obviously it is more profitable for the mines to sell gold on the open market than it is to sell to the Royal Canadian Mint and thus become eligible for assistance under the act.
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
One of the prime questions, I suppose, facing both the mining community and the international community today is what is the prospect for the long-range price of gold. There are really two factors influencing this. First of all, there is the impact of the uncertainty in international monetary relations, an uncertainty which, in the period since about the middle of last year, has brought about a dramatic increase in the price of gold on the open market.
As an example of this, on January 15 of this year gold was at a price of around $65 per ounce on the open market. By February 15 it had moved to between $72 and $73 per ounce. By March 15 it was up to $82, and my information today, March 29, is that it was over $89. It has been higher than that in the last several days.
Therefore this indicates that the instability of the international monetary exchanges has undoubtedly affected the external price of gold. Notable international commentators like Mr. Elliott Janeway have predicted that the price of gold will probably go up to a level of $130 per ounce. I express no opinion on that, but it is that kind of information and feeling that undoubtedly have had some kind of speculative impact on the price of the product itself.
That, however, has not been the only thing. Demand for the commodity on a commercial basis for commercial uses, such as for jewellery, industrial and other uses, has been increasing. In the same period world output of gold has declined. Last year world output of gold declined by about 6.5 per cent. So influencing the price of gold is a combination of speculation in relation to international financial affairs and the ordinary pressures exerted by supply of and demand for gold, not as a monetary commodity but as an industrial commodity.
Therefore it is obviously difficult to predict the future price of gold in the open market. However, it is possible that if there is a lot of fluctuation in gold prices as a result of monetary speculation there will be declines for short periods to the point where continued operation of gold mines that are still in the position to draw assistance would be in jeopardy. It is with this possibility in mind that the government has responded to the requests of the industry and the gold mining communities for assurance that assistance under the act will be available if needed.
The total amount of assistance paid under the act since it came into effect in 1948 is $303,188,031. From this may be deducted the sum of $25.7 million which the Royal Canadian Mint has received as a profit from the sale of gold on the open market during the years 1968 to 1971. Because of the high open market price for gold there were in fact no applications for assistance received from the gold mines with respect to the calendar year 1972.
As I have mentioned, details of assistance paid in total and to individual mine operators may be found in the annual report on the administration of the act which I tabled in the House on January 4. Perhaps some indication of the effectiveness of the program in the period since 1948 may be found in table one of this report, which indicates that 117 mines were drawing assistance in 1948. By 1971 this number had dropped to 28, and there has been a distinct contraction in the Canadian gold mining industry during that period.

March 29, 1973
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
I believe it is fair to say that the act has achieved the objective of minimizing the social and economic impact that would have occurred in the dependent communities with the abrupt closure of gold mines through the cushioning effect that may be achieved by slowing the rate of decline in the gold mining industry. This has always been the underlying motive behind the program.
A corollary to this program is, of course, the efforts that have been taken by the federal and provincial governments to develop alternative economic opportunities in the gold mining areas that are most affected. I suppose the classic example of success here has been in the neighbourhood of Timmins, where one saw the gradual decline of the gold mining industry in that area and then the dramatic revival of the community through the discovery of copper by Texas Gulf Sulphur and the subsequent establishment of further processing facilities in that community.
On August 11, 1970, my predecessor, the Hon. J. J. Greene, announced that the government of Canada had decided to extend the application of the statute for a further period of two and a half years, to June 30, 1973. There was no change made in the method of giving assistance. The minister also announced that the government of Canada was prepared to consider a second extension for an additional two and a half years to December 31, 1975, provided that suitable adjustment programs for the gold mining communities involved could be developed in cooperation with the provincial governments, the communities, the companies and the unions concerned.
In pursuance of this goal the minister met in Ottawa with representatives of the mining industry, the provincial governments of Ontario and Quebec and, of course, officials of the department on May 20 and 21, 1971, to identify and recommend scientific and technical programs that might lead to an acceleration in the rate of discovery and development to broaden the economic base of the regions. As a result of this Ottawa workshop the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announced on June 30, 1971, that a special scientific and technical effort would be mounted in those areas of his department. The governments of Ontario and Quebec also announced measures to stimulate exploration in the areas concerned.
While the increased price of gold affords new signs of hope for some 14 communities still largely dependent on this industry in Canada, labour unions, the municipalities concerned, mining companies operating in those communities and, of course, provincial governments all have to continue, in the very real initiative shown so far, to expand economic activity in these areas.
The government of Canada, through my department and an interdepartmental committee working with representatives both of the industry and of the two provincial governments, has arrived at a set of priorities for exploration and prospecting programs. It was the choice of the province of Ontario, at its option, to go for the provision of special subsidies for exploration and prospecting. The province of Quebec, on the other hand, decided to launch a large geoscience program, including geochemistry and geophysics, funded jointly with the federal department of Regional Economic Expansion.

It would be comforting, but I think unrealistic, to suggest that the problems of our gold mining communities will vanish overnight because the official gold price has been raised to $38 from $35 as a result of the earlier devaluation. At the moment the United State Congress has not acted on the most recent valuation and it is premature, therefore, to say what the established official price will be. I think we can recognize, however, the destabilizing influences that international markets can have on our resource communities and the need to devise continued policies and programs which will broaden the economic base of Canada's mining communities.
Consequently, the government will pursue its efforts in co-operation with other interested parties to assist the gold mining communities in their adjustment to changing circumstances. As part of that program it is appropriate to provide some assurance of future stability to gold mining operations and to the dependent communities by extending the operation of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to June 30, 1976. What we propose to do in this period of relatively high price is maintain a floor that is established by statute in the event that as a result of the vicissitudes of the international market the price might again change, creating another emergency condition.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO JUNE 30, 1976
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the remarks of the minister in support of the bill before us today, and I think it is relevant to again reiterate, as he has, that some 14 communities in Canada are to a large extent dependent upon the maintenance of this industry in a healthy condition. It should also be pointed out that Canada, perhaps inadvertently, has fared very well in respect of its gold holding over the last few years.
As the minister pointed out, the world price of gold has shot up in recent weeks, but it is not yet clear what ultimate price it will attain. At the present time it is well for the House to bear in mind that at the end of February our official international reserves of gold amounted to $834.1 million. That figure is expressed at the prevailing rate of $38 per ounce. As the minister pointed out, it is virtually a certainty that the price will be adjusted to $42.22 per ounce. When that takes place we will find that the value of our gold holdings in our official international reserves in Canada will increase to $926.8 million. If we work back from that adjusted figure of $926.8 million which, if it is not reflected in the March Bank of Canada Review, in all likelihood will be reflected in the April Review, we find that the actual increase in value of our gold holdings in our reserves has been $158.6 million since May of last year. In short, Canada was a real winner as far as monetary holdings of gold are concerned.
A point that is perhaps overlooked is the fact that if the world market for gold is relevant at today's price, which on the London bullion market was $89.25 per ounce, our actual holding of gold are worth $1.9 billion. This is a windfall for Canada of some $1 billion. It is the result of our holding gold in our international reserves, possibly inadvertently, at the right time.
I would also point out, as the minister has stated, that the actual outflow in assistance to the mines since this act
March 29, 1973

was proclaimed is approximately $278 million. The minister did not mention that if we take into account the increase in the value of our international reserve, the $158.6 million I mentioned, the net outlay, taking both things into account, is $120 million. Canada, as a result of having the foresight to institute and keep this act effective, has spent a net of $120 million, yet today it has reaped a $1 billion benefit in terms of world prices, if the market becomes free at some later date and our reserves of gold can be sold into that world market at today's prices.
I am stressing the fact that this act is doubly beneficial in that it has not only helped to preserve a worth while industry in Canada, which employs some 3,000 people directly at the present time and, assuming there are three and a half people indirectly employed to one directly employed, in the neighbourhood of 10,000 to 12,000 jobs, but in addition it has resulted in our having the advantage of holding a large amount of gold in our international reserves. This strengthens our world position tremendously. In that regard, it is often forgotten that while our production in relative terms is small, we are the second largest gold producer in the free world. South Africa is the largest producer and is greatly ahead of us. It produces approximately 70 per cent of the free world gold, but we are the second largest. I should emphasize that our production has been lessening year by year. Canadian production of gold in 1972 was valued at $76 million while in 1971 it was almost $80 million.
I feel, as does my party, that we should maintain our gold industry, and it is desirable that this act be extended in order to allow forward planning in the industry in the future. We believe this is the mechanism through which the government can assure this industry a minimum price at which it can sell its product. This is desirable when you are encouraging people to take advantage of world prices and to capitalize on those prices referred to by the minister.
In reference to how high the price might go the minister said that Mr. Janeway feels it might increase to $130 an ounce. That may be so, but I should like to refer to the 1972 annual bullion report of Samuel Montagu and Company Limited. Samuel Montagu and Company Limited is one of the largest London, England, bullion dealers. After reviewing the uncertainties in the monetary system today Samuel Montagu states:
Under the circumstances it is difficult to imagine a return of confidence and with the probability of recurring crisis prices in excess of $100 may easily be reached.
I feel, therefore, we are fortunate in this country that we do have producing mines in the gold field. I think we are even more fortunate to know there are additional prospects and additional possibilities that mines may be opened up if the industry has the assurance that it in fact will not have the ground cut from under it in its long-range planning. This is where I feel the act is a great help in that it gives them that assurance. While in a moment or so I will have some comments on matters that we feel could be considered by the committee, I want to assure the House that we are in support of having this type of legislation extended.
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
I would also like to touch on the question of production in the industry. I could give figures-some of them perhaps have already been touched on-concerning Canada's production in relation to world figures. Without delaying this debate, I think it is interesting to note that Canada, mining men inform me, is in a position to be able to increase, percentage wise, its gold production more than is any other country in the free world. Already there is a renewed confidence being shown with regard to gold mining. For example, the gold mining index on the Toronto Stock Exchange today was 231 compared with a low of 140 in 1972. I believe this is due partly to the fact that the industry knows this type of act will likely be passed by parliament. This has helped to renew confidence in the industry itself. Today's price is, of course, the main stimulant.
If I may I should like to come to the points I wish to suggest the committee of parliament should consider when this bill is referred to it. I would mention first that we feel the committee should consider whether June 1976, is a desirable termination date for this bill. It may be that it would be wiser to give the industry a longer term assurance of our intentions. It may be the industry could be assured that until say 1980 this type of assistance will be available to it if it wishes to make plans for the future production of existing mines or the bringing into existence of new mines.
We would like the committee to at least consider the provision put in the act in 1963 which limited the application of the act to what are called established mining communities. As I understand it, at the present time the act does not apply to a gold mine unless it is deemed to provide support in a designated community and unless more than 50 per cent of the persons employed in the mine reside in one of the established mining communities listed in a schedule to the act. We question whether it is desirable to limit this type of act to that extent. It may be-and I certainly suggest it should be-looked into by the committee.
Again, the minister in his opening comments mentioned that the bill does not contemplate the changing of the method of payment in respect of assistance. We feel the committee should review this also in that we must bear in mind that if the assistance is to be meaningful it surely must take into account the inflationary problems this country is living with. If this is to be realistic assistance we feel it is foolish to leave the assistance at too low a level.
At the present time I understand that if gold sells for roughly $50 an ounce or more on world markets it is not necessary for any company or mine in Canada to resort to this act but that, if the price should fall below that figure, in some cases companies might apply for the assistance. I am suggesting the committee should take a look and see whether the $49-$50 figure is a realistic point for this act to become effective.
Again-and the minister has commented on this-we feel greater stress should be put on encouraging exploration and prospecting in the mining industry including the gold mining field. I believe one of the problems in prospecting and exploration at the present time is certain unfavourable provisions in the Income Tax Act. I think

March 29, 1973
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
this should be reviewed when we consider the bill at the committee level. In short, we feel encouragement should be given to this type of industry in order to ensure that we are and will remain a significant producer in terms of world markets and in terms of our own production.
As my final point I would suggest the committee might consider the name of the bill itself. It is called the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I feel that is a misnomer at the present time; certainly I hope it is in the sense of the word "emergency". It may be that the committee could consider a more appropriate name for the act to indicate to the industry, to the gold mining companies of the country, that we are serious in our long-range thinking concerning this field and that we will give them not a short-range commitment with regard to a floor price, if you like to call it that, but rather a much longer range commitment with regard to where we stand and also a broader range of assistance in such fields to which I have referred as exploration and prospecting. Let us help to develop any mines that may be capable of development in Canada. We hope this legislation will receive speedy passage and we certainly look forward to being able to go into the matter in greater depth when it reaches the committee.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO JUNE 30, 1976
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this matter comes up at five-year intervals this is probably the fourth time I have had the opportunity to support this piece of emergency legislation. Over the years I have done so for various reasons which have not always been the same. Originally I came out of the gold mining industry and therefore was aware of the archaic form of management that existed in that industry and the lack of ability management had in dealing with the community or with its employees or in fact with anyone else. This, of course, stems not only from the personnel in the industry but also from the fact that they were rich when everybody else in the country was poor. Not unlike the landed gentry class in other countries, they developed a type of management that was difficult to support under any circumstances. I have changed my mind as the attitude of the industry has changed. Certainly the industry is in dire need of assistance to keep it alive and, in turn, and much more important, to keep the communities alive where it operates.
It was interesting to hear the last speaker, and I hope I am not unkind to him when I say he speaks with the voice of the business entrepreneur. I know his connections in the financial world, and I presume his interest is in the field of economics rather than in the individual mines that have closed and the individual miners who have left the industry. However, he raised a point that should be considered even though I do not think we will do anything about it.
We hold almost $850 million worth of gold in Canada. If we put it on the international market at $100 an ounce, or as that hon. member said, at $70 an ounce, Canada would stand to gain at least $1 billion and possibly $2 billion. I stress that we are not holding a very large quantity of gold in Canada. From 1948 to 1971 we have paid just over $301 million in assistance to gold producers. If we sold our present stock on the international market we could recov-

er all of that and still have twice as much left over. But obviously we will not do that. If we sell the gold we now have it will be at a maximum price of $42 because that is the maximum amount the Americans will agree to pay. Some big deal, Mr. Speaker! Gold is selling on the market in London at $90 an ounce and in other markets at well over $100 an ounce.
The government has paid a fortune to support the American dollar. No doubt the previous speaker could indicate just how much. Just recently I thought we had reached a new low when I noticed a hostess in the parliamentary restaurant open a roll of quarters. Only three of the coins were Canadian; the rest were all American. Obviously we are still selling our coinage to the United States to be melted down, because before 1968 our coins contained 80 per cent silver and as a result they are now worth much more than 25 cents for each quarter.
A number of mine managers have indicated to me that probably a third force will enter the situation and bring some stability to the price of gold. That third force would be a coalition between Russia and South Africa. As a gold producer Canada plays a small role in comparison with those two countries.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) will remember that when he made wheat sales to Russia payment for them was received in gold. That was when gold was $35 an ounce. But we did not keep that gold. We immediately traded it to the United States so we would not upset the money market.
We are penalizing a whole industry by trying to uphold the American dollar and the American way of life. Eventually somebody will make a change, and the price of gold will be stabilized at a reasonable rate. When that stabilization takes place it will probably be at the expense of the United States, which for many years cheated us on the price of gold by maintaining the price at a level that was not compatible with the cost of production.
Over the years we have paid more than $300 million to support some 84 mines that were initially covered by this program in 1948. At present there are 21 mines operating under the provisions of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. The time may come when the production of gold will be undertaken in other mines, and this act should be applicable to them. At present its provisions do not cover new mines. Two or three new mines have been opened in Ontario and a similar number in Quebec, and they are not covered by this legislation. About 1958 the act was amended to prevent its application to new mines.
I support this legislation for two reasons. It is an insurance policy that from now on will not cost the Canadian people any money. As a result of the last revision of the act, mines must co-operate with Canada Manpower in placing employees, some four months in advance of any closure of operations. In Ontario we operate under the Labour Standards Act, but this does not make any difference. However, I am sure all the provinces do not have the same legislation. Further, the committee set up by a previous minister, the hon. Mr. Greene, has been an asset to the miners in the industry.
This is an old industry. Most of the mines are old. Most of them have a limited foreseeable future, no matter what
March 29, 1973

the price of gold may be, but there are new areas that could be developed if the price of gold can be stabilized in the neighbourhood of $100 an ounce.
The hon. member who preceded me said that tax cuts would also assist the industry. That is not the problem. The problem is that almost all of the ground in Northern Ontario, and I believe the same is true of Quebec, has been staked and restaked. Over the years some of it has been sold for payment of taxes. Transactions have taken place in many ways. But in recent years any worthwhile ground has been tied up by large mining companies which have bought up the patented claims and are sitting on them. I believe they will continue to sit on them for a considerable time to come. There is no worse example than Little Long Lac which came in, closed down the mine, liquidated the treasury and went some place else. Not much better is Noranda which also has very large tracts of ground that it holds almost in perpetuity because of the inability of the province of Ontario to make any real decision about making that land otherwise available.
The hon. member mentioned some assistance to prospectors and there certainly should be some. The minister mentioned the help given to the companies. That information all goes in the company files and the government records in such a form that most of the prospectors I know are not able to get much advantage out of it, particularly when prospecting is done with the modern up-to-date devices that are being used for mineral surveys.
It is surprising to note that most of the gold potential in Ontario was known almost at the beginning of the gold mining industry in Ontario. There have been very few finds that have not been listed on maps issued by the Department of Mines for probably 40 or 50 years. I know of no instance where a mine has been developed in which there was not previous knowledge of gold in that particular area.
The minister is relatively new in a department that has had a great deal of difficulty in justifying the payments it has made. This assistance has been a direct handout to an industry. It was never tied to the wages in the area, was never, until the last amendment, tied to the communities, and was not tied to the national interest in any way. It was a handout to the mines for the purpose of their making a decision whether or not they could carry on.
I agree wholeheartedly that the situation has reversed. Even the small amount of gold we hold can repay the Canadian people two or threefold for the expenditure that they made; certainly it can double the payment on the expenditure they made. This is a fairly tidy sum no matter how you look at it. The member who spoke previously indicated that probably a profit of $1 billion could be made on the $300 million paid out; that is a reasonable estimate and it may even go higher if we hold the gold.
I suggest to the minister that while we are in favour of this legislation not very much has been done by the committee that he mentioned involving the communities, three or four branches of government and the Ontario and Quebec governments in particular for the purpose of finding alternative industries for that area. I suggest that the subsidies paid to those secondary industries are more
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
than worthwhile. The boom taking place in Timmins today is related to the incentive that was developed by the finding of copper and zinc in that area but it is really being assisted by the fact that secondary industry is being developed in the form of processing of raw resources. In the end I believe this will produce a greater incentive for other types of industry.
Those who considered this subject in the initial committee which made reports from the gold mining communities to the minister of the day were well aware that the assistance was necessary to carry on for today but it really did not do anything for tomorrow. In some ways I am unhappy about the fact that the price of gold on the international market, where most of the mines are dealing, has gone up because it has relieved the mining industry of its responsibility to participate with community leaders and the provincial and federal governments in providing the incentive to look for other industries.
In my own area I was pleased the other day to go into a small plant which has nothing to do with the gold mining industry. This plant was given a DREE grant of $250,000 to produce 42 jobs. It has not met the criteria yet so has not received the money, but it has created 20 jobs. The production line has to be in full operation for 30 days in order to qualify for the grant and because it diversified the production line for different products it has not reached the 30 days. With the incentive and assistance that were given the plant was able to produce new products. The president of the company indicated that in the first year of operation they had already been able to show a fairly reasonable profit even though they have not yet received the full assistance promised them. Not only is the company providing a profit directly but it is producing a profit through the taxes paid by every one of its employees. There are 20 employees buying goods in that community.
The situation as to the age of miners in the gold mining industry has not changed. Two and a half years have gone by and they are two and a half years older. The ability to bring new people into the industry is limited because the production of many mines is limited. One of the two mines in the Kirkland area has closed in the last year and I am sure in the other gold mining communities there has been a decline. The number of mines has decreased from 28 to 21 in one year.
When the committee meets, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that it should give consideration to redeeming or at least reinvesting the amount of money the government now can make on the gold that it holds. If the government finds that this is not to its advantage, maybe it could be put into the northern mining communities in the form of a new subsidy. I think somewhat the same result would accrue- a greater return on the expenditure.
Some of our problems in Northern Ontario, are problems of the Ontario government. I am told that this has been changed in Quebec to some extent. In my part of Northern Ontario we are interested in reopening a great number of small mines. The town of Cobalt for some years has operated on two or three different mining systems. There is one large company that comes in and plays the stock market; others come in, do the development and actually do some mining. Most of the mining operations,
2742

March 29, 1973
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act however, are under a lease whereby they do the work underground, contract for the milling and employ eight or ten men. I suggest that this can happen in the gold mining industry.
At present there is an over-capacity of milling facilities in Northern Ontario and there are certainly a great number of mines that have been closed for a long period of time which have shafts for underground workings and would lend themselves to the type of lease operations whereby someone with a reasonably small amount of capital could start mining the ore. A custom mill operation could be set up and the end product could be sold after it had been processed by that custom mill. It seems to me that this would provide a large source of employment for miners. In addition, it would permit our people to enter a field that is exciting and holds out reasonable expectations of profit. That would suit the character and nature of our people who have been pioneers, willing to gamble and willing to engage in ventures that hold out an opportunity of profit provided that the necessary hard work is done. This cannot be done, however, until we do something about the holding rights of large companies that own large blocks of land. The minister and the committee ought to consider that question. It is of interdepartmental importance because it involves relationships between the provinces. I hope that when the two and a half years have expired our gold mining industry will not be in the position we thought it was in two or three years ago. I hope that our gold mining industry will prosper and that Canada again will be among the leading producers of gold ore.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO JUNE 30, 1976
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about Bill C-130, an Act to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
Mr. Speaker, gold mines are now in a good financial position because the current price of gold on the free market has reached $90 an ounce, but, as a consequence, gold mine operators have had to increase salaries considerably. In 1971, it was nearly impossible to find experienced miners willing to work for $2.43 an hour. But in 1973, the salaries are close to those in other industries. Thanks to plenty of manpower and the new price of gold, many mines would like to invest in operating and expanding the mines, which would create thousands of jobs.
Mr. Speaker, with the instability of the price of gold, it is nearly impossible for the mines to expand. At present, the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act is in force and it does not cost a cent to the government.
I find strange that the government has decided to continue giving subsidies to gold mining until 1976. In the past, delegations from my constituency and from other areas of Canada came to Ottawa every two years with briefs for the minister, asking him to retain the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, yet today the minister appears so generous by wanting the law applied until 1976.
Mr. Speaker, I fail to see why the minister does not increase the subsidies to $18 or $20 an ounce: it would not
.'Mr. Peters.]
cost anything and it would give some guarantee to the gold mines. .
Mr. Speaker, I met some gold mine managers to find out what they think about the new bill. As I said a while ago, they are willing to expand, to operate, but they have been given no guarantee. This is what they told me: If we had a guarantee that the price of gold would not go down below $60 an ounce, we could keep on improving the situation in the mines. But now we have no guarantee.
I therefore recommend that the committee urge the minister and the government to increase the subsidies to $18 or $20 an ounce, which would give the gold mines a minimum guarantee of $60 an ounce.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO JUNE 30, 1976
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) says he has heard debates like the present one over a long period of time. So have I. I recall his speaking in 1958, and his message still concerns one theme, the interests of the communities and workers in the mining areas.
My opening words in the debate on this amendment are that the name of the act is a misnomer. We call the act the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. It has been in existence for nearly 30 years. Some emergency! As the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) made dramatically clear, Canada has been handed a windfall. To use the crude expression used by the military during the war, we are like someone who fell into an outhouse and came out smelling like roses. We certainly have come out of the situation in wonderful financial shape.
The theme of my remarks will be, what lessons should we learn from this fortuitous happening that has added so greatly to the monetary and financial assets of the people of Canada? I will come around in full circle as I talk about these lessons to some of the remarks I have heard the hon. member for Timiskaming make concerning development during the last 15 years. Before I do that, however, I want to talk about something the minister and the hon. member for York-Simcoe mentioned, stabilization.
The first lesson that the legislators of this country must learn is that the stabilizing of prices of basic world commodities is no longer something to be dreamed about or practised now and then but something to be practised systematically. We should recognize that certain products are inelastic in nature and very necessary to the world, and we should begin to build through legislation a price structure for those products. The value of such stability to producers is obvious. We are now recognizing with brutal clarity that consumers of goods around the world are taking a terrible beating because of the failure not only of the government of Canada but of many governments of the world to stabilize commodity prices through legislation. I am referring to legislation dealing with basic world products. We, in Canada, have had the lesson dramatically brought home to us with regard to food products. Planning has been based on mistaken notions of world demand. As a result, Canada, the United States and other countries are critically short of basic commodities with which to feed their people, not to mention the other peoples of the world.
March 29, 1973

Every bit as important as food in the provision of a better way of life for the peoples of the world are the basic products which are absolutely vital to the future success of industrialization in newly developing countries. Gold is one of those inelastic commodities to which I referred. Copper is another. Such inelastic commodities are vital to the carrying out of the world's business and the development of the world's industries. When their prices rise too precipitously, the newly developing nations are forced to spend so much of their international exchange in purchasing these products that all the good that has been provided since the war through the over $100 million in bilateral programs by the wealthier nations trying to help these nations has been wiped out two or three times over by the rise in price of these inelastic commodities.
The first principle the committee should work on is the principle enunciated by the hon. member for York-Simcoe. Now that we have come through this period of emergency for 30 years, let us take a look at the principle of stabilization and see if we can put this principle into the bill in order to give some assurance to the mining industry on the business side, as the hon. member for York-Simcoe said, and also with regard to the labour component. Because of the precarious position of gold prices these past 30 years, families in these communities have had to eke out an existence at levels of wages far below the minimum standards even available in these northern communities where costs are so much higher. The principle of stabilization would not only benefit the producers in the form of management, the owners, if you like, and the labour component but it would also be in the general interest of bringing some help to people all over the world who need stability with regard to these inelastic commodities. That is a principle we could well adopt. That is the first suggestion, thought or thrust that will come forward in committee if the party on this side of the aisle has its way.
I now want to discuss a point raised by the minister when he spoke about international monetary arrangements having such an impact on the situation in relation to the present gold mining industry in Canada. I think it is a bit beyond the terms of reference of the committee to which this legislation is being sent to discuss this, but it has a bearing and I will raise it in any event. I refer to the fact that by this windfall there has been an increase in the genuine price of the gold in our international reserves to over $1 billion, and it will probably be more before the price levels off. We should be thinking about how we can best utilize this excess or increase of money in trying to increase the whole industrial fabric of our country and at the same time help our neighbours and customers all around the world.
One thought that passed through the minds of some people this past year was that with our tremendous surplus of almost useless American dollars in our reserve fund, now buttressed by the doubling of the value of the gold in our reserve fund, we should begin thinking in terms of previous precedents in this regard. We should put some of these American dollars, which are only yielding us a little over 5 per cent, into the purchase of equities
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
of large multinational companies, mainly those with headquarters in the United States. I say the United States mainly because the health of the gold mining industry and the health of all our exporting industries are dependent on getting our dollar down to a value roughly equivalent to the true balance of trade between our two nations.
We have large investments from the United States, mostly in the form of investments in multinational companies. These bother and concern the Canadian people, and rightfully so. If we were to move $1 billion into the purchase of equities-some people prefer bonds but it makes no difference-this would provide a flow of those almost useless dollars back to the American side. This would have the effect of bringing down our dollar to about 95 cents. We could establish this value by the amount of purchases.
There are other advantages. First, we have the useless American dollar. It is only $4 billion of the $70 or $90 billion available in the reserve funds of many countries, but we could put these assets to work. From the ownership of these equities we would not only get the dividends flowing back into Canada to balance the flow of our dividends to the United States but we would get the appreciation of their capital value. Above all, this would give to the people of Canada a sense of assurance and security by recognizing that the multinational corporation is here to stay.
We recognize the tremendous power, strength and good this can bring to the nations of the world in facilitating trade. Nothing will stop their economic efficiency, but the people of Canada would feel happier if they owned a good chunk of General Motors, XEROX, IBM, machinery companies and so on. Over a period of years we could come very close to a substantial controlling influence over the multinational companies that currently own so much of Canadian industry. I hope this policy will appeal to countries like Japan, West Germany, France and Switzerland which hold so many so-called useless American dollars in their reserve funds. Not only would we be helping Canadians but we would also be helping our friends and customers, the Americans.
There are two well known precedents for this. In 1914, when our comrades in the United Kingdom got into trouble with the Kaiser, it was the Americans who came to their help. They provided them with the dollars. In return, the Americans took the equities that United Kingdom residents owned around the world. As a result, the United Kingdom was able to survive the war of 1914-18. When the war was over the American people owned the bulk of their equities around the world. This formed the basis for the present large proportion of multinational companies that seem to dominate and seem to be able to dominate the ownership and control of products around the world.
I think the clock has now turned full circle. If we would use the excess American dollars in our treasury and utilize the extra value of our gold by buying either equities or bonds, and they are there now, we could not only help ourselves but bring help to the American people in their hour of need. They are going to be in need for, I think, at least another decade. I have references to support this view. One of the better known American bankers in Chicago stated publicly that if the Canadians are not
2744

March 29, 1973
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
smart enough to do this the American government should buy up equities on the Wall Street market and provide them for our exchange funds in lieu of sending their dollars here.
The United States is desperately short of dollars. Their international liquidity is quite tight. Canadians, for intelligent self-interest, should think in terms of helping the Americans in their hour of difficulty. If, after 20 or 30 years, we end up owning, with our tremendous saving power in Canada, big blocks of these multi-national corporations, with their tremendous earning power we will have moved and moved well for Canada.
This seems a long way from the usual type of debate that we have on the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I simply wish to say that it is very pleasant to be in the House at a time when our fortunes have turned so much in our favour. I hope we can take advantage of these lessons and use them for good purposes.
The second suggestion I want to make deals with communities. There is no question in my mind that in our efforts to save the gold mining industry we thought just in terms of keeping that industry alive on a bare existence level. The people who have suffered are the families of the workers and those who serviced these workers in remote northern areas of Canada. Another lesson we should learn from this windfall is that we should begin thinking seriously of placing revenues derived from our nonrenewable resources into development funds, the principal to be used only for the development of this country; all the Canadian public should have the right to dispose of would be the interest or dividends from its investment. Such is the tremendous volume of wealth that would come from our resource industries in the non-renewable sector that within a very few years a fund amounting to many billions of dollars would have been established and the interest from it would be much greater each year than the annual revenue from the sale of those resources. In other words, we should think of our resources as belonging not only to this generation but to many other succeeding generations. Such a fund as I have suggested could be operated by the government alone, or it could be operated in co-operation with private industry. I would hope that once the program was under way, the government would get out.
When this measure is referred to committee I believe we should look at this legislation not merely as a makeshift to enable us to get by for another three years but as an opportunity to establish something of more permanent value. Consider the name of the legislation. Consider the principle of the legislation-stabilization. Consider its impact on monetary affairs, not only of this country but of the world. We should recognize that sometimes, when we are trying to keep an industry alive, especially when that industry is providing a product that is needed, we end by benefiting not only ourselves but the whole world. If we approach the legislation from this point of view we can introduce a concern for stabilization which can be applied to other products of the resource industry whose supply is inelastic and which are so needed by the people of the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take part briefly in the debate on Bill C-130. I should like to draw the attention of the minister to one or two aspects which so far have not been raised.
I was here in 1970 and was a member of the committee that dealt with the bill before us at that time. I believe you were a member of that committee, too, Mr. Deputy Speaker. At that time suggestions were put forward not only by members of the committee but by senior civil servants that the government should be moving into these mining communities and endeavouring to lay out programs which would make them less dependent on the gold mining industry. Going through the notes I made at that time I see that an interdepartmental study was proposed early in 1970 along the very lines to which I have drawn attention. It was suggested that the various departments of government concerned get together with the municipalities, mining companies and unions in an effort to devise a plan to diversify industry in these mining communities. One of the witnesses at that committee hearing put on record three recommendations which apparently had been made in a report to the government of the day. They were as follows:
(a)	Co-ordinate activities within the federal government, industry and the unions;
(b)	Establish a firm federal position and enter into negotiation with other parties; and
(c)	Undertake an ongoing appraisal of developments in the communities and the effectiveness of various programs.
He added that an interdepartmental committee had been established but had not yet made any concrete proposals.
I ask the minister what he has done, or what his department has done, or what his predecessor has done to follow up this suggestion which was made in 1970. The committee at that time approved an extension of the legislation to 1975, if necessary, on the basis that the committee to which I have referred would be taking certain action and making recommendations in the hope that something permanent could be achieved in areas where gold mining is the basic industry.
In endorse the bill and intend to vote for it, believing it would be unwise at this time to do anything that might upset areas where gold mining is on the verge of going out of business. We have enough unemployment in Canada as it is and, as the minister said earlier in his speech, the price of gold is so high now that the companies concerned would be foolish to sell to anyone except on the open market. After the $45 per ounce production cost has been met they get no increase in assistance from the fund.
I urge the minister to tell us, either in his closing speech or during the committee stage, what progress, if any, has been made in the effort to bring other industries into gold mining communities. The situation presently is an example of what has happened as a result of Canada's failure over the years to establish basic secondary industries in communities where the raw materials are produced, though I agree that gold mining is somewhat different from other mining operations. But whether in lead, zinc or other fields the need is to set up extensive job-intensive secondary industries in areas where these raw materials are produced. I will close on that note, but during the
March 29, 1973

committee stage I will come back with a number of questions, and I hope to pursue the line on which I have suggested the minister provide information.
