speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) is proceeding to the House to participate in this debate. He is chairman of the committee to which the document is being referred, so we will await his remarks with some interest.
The question of how much information a government should make available to Members of Parliament is one that has bothered many governments and many Members of Parliament. The thirst of private members, both members of the opposition and government members, for information seems to be insatiable when it comes to documents. Of course, the more privileged a document in terms of government understanding, the more that document is required or wanted by members of the opposition. The matter really comes down to a question of balance. It does not matter what kind of regulations, written or unwritten, are in effect; it depends upon the way these regulations are administered and the way they are applied.
The difficulty we have in a parliamentary cabinet type system is that so much of the decision-making takes place in cabinet and other closed circles, and making documents available before a decision is made compounds the work of the government. The basic principle in respect of documents which we are discussing is that all documents

shall be made available. This, in Canadian parliamentary terms, is a considerable change from the practice that applied before. Before the practice was that a document being requested, if it was not inconvenient to the government, would be made available. We have reversed that principle and are now saying that any document which is requested ought to be released unless there is some overriding reason it should not be released.
It is quite true, as hon. members pointed out in the previous debate, that the exemptions the government claims are extensive. Nevertheless, if anyone takes a look at the private bills that have been presented to the House by the House leader of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), and also by a member of the NDP, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Mather), he will see that these bills also contain a sizeable number of exemptions.
Why should this be so? I suggest it is so because those gentlemen do realize that not all information can be made available and, even where it can be made available, there ought to be some room for discretion in the interests of security of the state and for other good reasons.
One thing that frequently crops up in debates of this kind is reference to other countries. We are urged to look at other countries and model ourselves and our behaviour upon principles which are unique or acceptable to countries other than our own. So it was in the previous debate when we were urged to look at the system that functions in Sweden, where it is claimed that all documents are made available to the Swedish public with no restriction or with very few restrictions. That, of course, is nonsense.
In the intervening period of time I have had an opportunity of looking into the way in which the Swedish system works and of finding out what kind of restrictions they have and how they are applied. At the same time I have also had an opportunity of looking at the way the United States applies procedures for the release of documents.
Generally speaking, the Swedish principle is that documents should be made available without restraint. However, there are examples of cases where the authorities will decide a document does not have to be released. There are appeal provisions and appeals are heard by a form of administration court. However, I draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that the refusal to release a document by a cabinet minister is not appealable. Any cabinet minister in Sweden who refuses to release a cabinet document does not have to release it and there is no appeal from his decision. In many respects that is the application of a far more stringent doctrine of secrecy than anything Canada has, and certainly under the proposed guidelines our concept is light years away from the one which applies at the political level in Sweden.
In addition, there is a comment that should be made about secrecy and confidentiality of the workings of the governmental process. It is a well known fact that the effective functioning of government requires the use of confidences between different parts and agencies of the government. It is also a well known fact that if these confidences are not respected the machinery of government begins to break down. The difficulty in putting things on the record on a confidential basis is that if these
March 29, 1973

confidences are violated you reach the point where the government, the cabinet in particular, can no longer be assured of getting the best advice in confidence that it requires to make decisions. This applies to interpretations of what is going on in the government and its agencies and also interpretations of government relationships with other countries and provinces in a federal system. It also applies to interpretation of the ability of individual people and agencies, so there can be on that basis alone a whole host of exemptions.
In Sweden this policy applies in a general way, but as a result of Swedish law where the spirit is to release documentation there has been a development toward a form of oral briefing rather than putting the information on paper. The reason is, of course, that if a briefing is oral the information conveyed is in an oral form and obviously cannot be produced in a meaningful way before a House of Commons or to a citizen who requests it. What this does, in fact, is destroy to some extent the reliability of the information being communicated because there is no way of checking out that information except in so far as the person who is giving it or receiving it is capable in the oral tradition. Fortunately, in our society that does not happen to be the case. It might be said that, as a result of this extensive freedom the Swedish government has accepted and applied, the greater use of personal meetings and oral presentations means that far less information is being presented to the government and the public, and to some extent the quality of decision-making and work going into presentations has been deteriorating.
It would seem that a close look at the Swedish system would indicate basically what the government has proposed in its guidelines is quite close and similar. It would also be fair to say that, just as good law can be ruined by inept application, bad law can be made to seem much better by the application of the law and regulations. So it is the spirit behind the regulations permitting production and release of documents that is more important than any written or agreed upon guidelines.
It is in this sense that the changes and guidelines the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) has introduced to the House of Commons are most significant. They take the position of the government of Canada from that of being secretive, releasing documents only at its own whim, to the position that it accepts the principle that documents ought to be and should be released, exempting only those that fall into a limited sort of exemption.
It is possible to look at the way the United States and Sweden have operated their systems to find out what kind of exemptions they have accepted and what kind of exemptions we are proposing in these guidelines to the House of Commons. Perhaps I might run through a brief table of these to indicate to hon. members which are accepted and which are not accepted as between the United States and Sweden.
For example, legal opinions or advice provided for the use of the government are available for release both in Sweden and in the United States. Papers, the release of which would be detrimental to the security of the state, are not released in either the United States or in Sweden. In respect of papers dealing with international relations, again both countries do not permit their release. Concern-
Motions for Papers
ing papers, the release of which might be detrimental to the future conduct of federal-provincial relations, this is not a problem of course in Sweden. In the United States system, because it is a federation, these are released. In respect of papers containing information the release of which would allow or result in direct personal financial gain or loss by a person or a group of persons, neither Sweden or the United States releases them. With regard to papers reflecting on the personal competence or character of an individual, neither country releases these. Papers of a voluminous character or which would require an inordinate cost or length of time to produce are released by both the United States and Sweden, but I understand that the person who requests them must pay the cost of producing them, which thereby acts as a very effective check. In respect of papers relating to the business of the Senate, Sweden does not have a senate and the United States has nothing on that.
With regard to papers, the release of which would be personally embarrassing to Her Majesty or the Royal Family or official representatives of Her Majesty, Sweden does have a monarchy and the United States not, but in the case of Sweden they apparently would release these papers if available. Papers relating to negotiations leading up to a contract, until the contract has been executed or the negotiations have been concluded, are refused both in Sweden and the United States. Then we have cabinet documents and those documents which include Privy Council confidence. Sweden would release them and the United States would release them, but again I draw attention to the different nature of government in these cases. The proper example in our case would be to compare our situation with that of Great Britain. In Great Britain these documents are not released either. In respect of any proceedings before a court of justice or a judicial inquiry of any sort, both the United States and Sweden refuse to release these documents. Sweden does release and the United States does not release internal departmental memoranda. In the case of papers requested, submitted or received in confidence by the government from sources outside the government, these are released by Sweden but not by the United States.
The point I am trying to make is that the principle the government has accepted in respect of the release of documents is a new one for Canada. These exemptions that the government claims are those which stand on their own; for example, those which have to do with papers which would come from the Royal Family or from the Governor General or which apply to the particular nature of Canada as a federal country in which the powers are split more or less between two centres. I feel this is a significant step. I think I can assure the House, as I have some responsibility for the application of the guidelines, that every attempt is being made to make as much information available to hon. members as we can within the scope of the guidelines. I think there will be increasing use of the formula that papers will be released subject to the reservation in respect of confidential documents and other matters that are confidential that these not be included in the papers to be released. We are certainly trying to take steps in that way.

Motions for Papers
As recently as Wednesday last we accepted three motions laid down by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) where some information requested was confidential. The papers have been gone through and the confidential parts have been removed. These papers will be available to the hon. member. Before these guidelines had been made such a motion would have been refused. I think because of the way in which the guidelines read and are being applied the result will be that Members of Parliament and the Canadian people will have access to far more material from the federal government than has been the case previously.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even on a rainy day I love to hear Liberals argue "ill-Liberal" principles. Of course, my friend's argument was destroyed today a little earlier in our proceedings when the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) was asked to make available to parliament a document which assessed the efficiency and so on of the opportunities for youth program, an important document to those of us who must consider the votes for the plan. The minister hid behind the usual phrase that the document was an internal document. No matter how good the guidelines are, if we have to put up with this it means that the guidelines are not guidelines or that the guidelines enunciated up to this point are much too restrictive. When governments talk about guaranteeing the security of the state in so far as secrecy or accessibility to information is concerned, the truth is that the guarantee and the fear are for the security of the government. This is not a bad objective, I presume, depending on where one sits. As I have said before, sometimes we are captured by our own rhetoric.
I think the United Kingdom really is a very bad example to use when we consider the whole matter of availability of documents and secrecy. They have worshipped far too long at the altar, if I can say that, of secrecy or anonymity. Being from Fundy-Royal, with my background I prefer looking at the French experience. Many senior civil servants in France not only are not anonymous but enunciate public policy quite freely. This is acceptable in the process of giving the public information about various policies. By a curious coincidence I was reading, because this whole matter is very much in the public mind in the United States as a result of the Ellsberg trials-presumably they are not sub judice in this place-that somebody had the good sense to take a look at what Dr. Johnson said. I am sure the minister is interested in Dr. Johnson. In 1756 Dr. Johnson in a book called "Observations on the Present State of Affairs" in so far as accuracy is concerned-and the state of affairs in 1756 was about the same as today- wrote:
The time is now come in which every Englishman expects to be informed of the national affairs; and in which he has a right to have that expectation gratified. For, whatever may be urged by ministers, or those whom vanity or interest makes the followers of ministers-
Presumably that includes parliamentary secretaries.
-concerning the necessity of confidence in our governours, and the presumption of prying with profane eyes into the recesses of policy, it is evident that this reverence can be claimed only by counsels yet unexecuted, and projects suspended in deliberation.
Dr. Johnson put it pretty grandly. But if we want to come to a contemporary critic of the British scene we find

one in Bernard Crick's Essays on Reform 1967. Included in these essays is an excellent comment by Professor J. A. G. Griffith in an article entitled "On Telling People". Professor Griffith says:
The wish to take the lid off the machinery of government, to see how it works, who says what to whom, at what level decisions are taken, what private criteria are used, how far 'politics' is allowed to override those criteria, on what statistical and other 'facts' the decisions are based: this wish does not derive only from curiosity or from party animosity but also from self-interest, from quis custodiet-
I translate that as a guardianship feeling, guardianship of the public interest.
-and from a feeling (by some) that governments represent another group interest.
A series of comments on the matter of secrecy was published in the London Times a few years ago in which the author listed various items. First, we should be told much more about the background against which decisions are taken. Second, there is a vast shaded area about which most of us know nothing but generally suspect the worst.
If the Secretary of State had released the report on the OFY program, I suspect the report would have relieved the mind of many people who now have every reason to be suspicious of the program. I believe that probably 98 per cent of the information marked "Restricted", "Secret" and "Confidential" would be so utterly boring that nobody would look at it anyway. In fact, I have met many officials in departments who themselves deplore the overuse of the labels "Restricted" and "Confidential."
In other countries, the passion for secrecy has not abated the cynicism of the public. We all have an obligation, as we try to arrive at ways to reform our procedures, really to believe in what we are doing and let the public have access to documents, with very few exceptions; in fact, a much narrower group of exceptions than the guidelines announced the other day.
Another point I wish to stress is that this year's estimates will show the largest amount ever spent by a government of this country on consultant services contracted outside the regular public service. I am not criticizing that situation particularly at the moment, because others will do so. But all through the estimates examples can be found of sums provided for consultant services, and practically all of them-even under the guidelines recently announced-will result in the information stemming from them being stamped, sealed and put away from public view. The only way to get information will be to wait for the inevitable leaks. There is no mystery about leaks: they occur when things are too watertight. When a government tries to run things in a restricted way, inevitably there are leaks. The way to end the leaks is to throw away the "Restricted" and the "Confidential" stamps except when matters go to the very security of the state or to the privacy of the individual.
Perhaps on another occasion we will have a chance to debate one or two more of the announced guidelines. Recently somebody told me that since the end of the Korean war the United States have amassed 450 billion restricted and confidential documents. I say, God help the
March 29, 1973

United States! What has happened, with the proliferation of confidential and secret documents, is that nobody can find anything anyway. This just shows the preposterous levels we have reached.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BRYDEN REPORT
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I will not repeat the comments I made on another motion some time ago when I tabled the guidelines that are to be referred to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments.
Probably, when guidelines are tabled indicating several categories of restrictions the immediate reaction is to feel, as one editorial put it, that the object is to tighten the screws and prevent information being made available. Perhaps presentationally, in the circumstances, in view of those categories, it was impossible to avoid that impression. However, in the cabinet, over the past several years, we have grappled with this problem in an effort to determine what basis there is, and ought to be, to withhold documents from publication.
We started with the laudable proposition of attempting as much as possible to run an open government and to make available as much information as could be made available. Because we started with that proposition, we attempted to examine the situation to find out whether we could make public at least the principles upon which our conduct was based. After a great deal of discussion we produced the guidelines and sent them to departments for their direction, and now we are sending them to a standing joint committee for examination to get the views of the committee on whether the guidelines indeed are sound in principle.
Is it sound, for example, to withhold legal opinions that the government receives? Is it sound to withhold information that is given to the government in confidence by an individual or by a corporation? Is it sound to withhold information or papers that might be embarrassing to Her Majesty? Is it sound to release papers, while contracts are being negotiated, that might have the effect of prejudicing
Motions for Papers
one party or the other? On many of these guidelines we reached the conclusion that in themselves they were soundly based. But we want the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments to examine the guidelines and have them fleshed-out by examples that might be produced by witnesses so that the committee may reach some conclusions.
I believe we are fortunate in having the joint committee available to take on this work, because of the status of the joint chairmen, the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) and the distinguished member of the other place. I am sure that the hon. member for Fundy-Royal is committed, as we all are, to obtaining the greatest possible availability of information and that he will examine the situation objectively with the members of the committee. We will have the benefit of their advice on whether, in certain cases, the guidelines are sound or can be elaborated on or developed in certain ways so that additional information can be made available.
I think the first question is: Are they sound in principle? The second question is: How are they to be administered? After all, an individual in a department, and ultimately the minister or the government, must decide in a particular case whether a document comes under the heading of a particular guideline.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BRYDEN REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a question? This is separate from the matter of the guidelines. Has the minister considered reviving a practice that used to be quite prevalent years ago in this House? When a member wanted a document produced, he was allowed to see it privately on his own good will and honesty that he would not quote directly from it. I recall times when we asked for documents and were allowed to see them privately, provided there were no direct quotes. I am not quarrelling with the government for not doing this, but has any consideration been given to it? I feel that the practice of the British House in this regard, of letting members see documents privately, would get around some of the problem.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BRYDEN REPORT
speechtext:
I think that is a good suggestion, Mr. Speaker. I am sure if this were done, hon. members would respect the confidentiality of the document. Possibly the committee could consider it and make some recommendations.
At a certain stage someone has to make the decision whether a document is to be produced. In the past, the decision was sometimes taken on very general grounds. In the guidelines, we are attempting to specify the grounds so that members will know why a document is being refused. I am aware that probably in the government generally, and certainly in departments, there has to be developed a greater awareness of parliament, the requirements of parliament and a much more responsible system of answering the questions of hon. members and their requests for the production of documents.
There was a system in the House by which motions for the production of papers were called during routine proceedings on certain days, and a vote was taken and the decision of the House was final. That procedure was found to be unsatisfactory and changes were made in the

March 29, 1973
Motions for Papers
rules, so that now if there is a desire on the part of a member or the government to proceed further, the motion is transferred for debate and it is possible to debate the issue. But normally it is not possible to reach a decision, for obvious reasons.
It may be that the committee could take that matter under consideration and determine whether at some point, retrospectively, a committee of the House ought to review the practice and whether refusal by the government in a particular case was justified, so that as we developed the procedure a more open system would be in existence and would be seen to be in existence.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal mentioned consultants' reports. There is no doubt that there has been a growth in the use of consultants, and as a result numerous motions have been put on the order paper asking for consultants' reports. There is no doubt that if you ask an individual in the government or outside for advice, if the advice is to be delivered privately it is couched differently than if the advice is to be delivered publicly. I have no doubt about the validity of that assertion, for obvious reasons.
We have now asked ministers who engage consultants to determine before the work is done whether it is expected that the report will be made public. If it is, the consultant ought to know so that he can defend the document in public. It seems somewhat unfair to ask an individual to make a report or give independent advice which he expects is to be rendered in private, and at a later stage to change the rules of the game and have the document made public. I hope that as a result of this specification in the guidelines, when consultants are engaged greater emphasis will be placed upon the practice of having the reports prepared so they can be made public, and that the consultant will know this when he begins his task.

speechtext:
Would the minister permit a question? Having produced these guidelines, I wonder whether he gave any consideration to listing the kinds of documents that would be tabled. He calls this document a set of guidelines, but to me it is more like the Ten Commandments: it tells you all the things you cannot do. This reminds me of the dear old lady who said that all they do is put ideas into one's head.
Why not a list of the kind of documents that would be tabled? It seems to me that we are not getting anywhere in this discussion, and maybe that is an argument in support of the matter going to committee. We all agree that everything possible should be tabled, but the minister gives negative guidelines that in the end say that something can be tabled but an awful lot would not be. Can the minister not produce something more positive than negative guidelines?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BRYDEN REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, probably it would have been a lot better if we had begun with 60 categories of documents that should be made public, then the 16 categories of exemptions would have appeared less suspicious to my hon. friend. The principle was that we proposed to make public everything that is available, with the exception of these restrictions. Looking at the guidelines, they do not encompass all the areas of government but there are rather specific areas included.

The committee may want to reverse the procedure and make a statement that is more positive, along the lines of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I realize I have mentioned that, presentationally, the conclusion or impression could have been created by the guidelines that the purpose was to tighten the situation. The opposite was the case. We wanted to open the flow of information, but in opening it we wanted to make clear to the House the principle that there ought to be exclusions. That is the point I made earlier and it is the point my parliamentary secretary made.
I had something to say about consultants' reports. I believe we would adopt a sounder approach if we could determine at the beginning what is to be made public, so that the man writing the report and giving advice would not be faced with the knowledge, several months later, that the document was to be made public. If that were the case, he would have a legitimate cause of complaint.
In the case of evaluation reports, it seems to me there is another difficulty and perhaps the committee would want to consider it. Departments are constantly evaluating their programs, either informally or in a formal way, and reports are produced for the use of the deputy minister or the minister. Persons making these reports are bound to be influenced by the knowledge that the reports are for the private use of officials. Are they to be made public for the use of all the people of Canada? I believe that if evaluation reports are to be made, it ought to be with a view to having them made public is such a request is ultimately made; but the request must be made that they be made public. Obviously, the same reasoning applies to other reports. I am sure many evaluations are made with the full knowledge, backed by a promise, that the reports are intended solely for the confidential use of officers within the department concerned.
