speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subsubtopic: REIMBURSEMENT TO PROVINCES FOR PARTIAL ADVANCES ON CROP INSURANCE PREMIUMS
speechtext:
that Bill C-129, to amend the Crop Insurance Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the Speech from the Throne reference was made to the government's intention to amend the Crop Insurance Act so that the cost to farmers of this protection would be reduced.
Bill C-129 provides that when a province agrees to increase its financial contribution to the program by paying all the administration costs, instead of being reimbursed to the extent of 50 per cent of these costs by the federal government, the federal government will increase its contribution to the premiums from 25 per cent to 50 per cent. In this way, both levels of government will increase assistance to farmers so as to reduce farmers' contributions from 75 per cent to 50 per cent of the premiums necessary to cover indemnities.
I have heard from the ministers of agriculture of all provinces which now have agreements with the federal government under the Crop Insurance Act and I am assured that this amendment has the endorsement of their respective governments. In fact, three provincial governments, British Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba, have recently made plans for their crop insurance agencies to sell crop insurance to farmers in 1973 using a rate structure based on the increased government contribution set out in this bill. Several other provinces planning to do so are hoping that this legislation will soon become law. It is understood that until this bill is passed, these provincial
Crop Insurance Act
governments will advance 50 per cent of the premium to the respective crop insurance funds and pay all administration costs.
The Crop Insurance Act was passed in 1959 and has been amended three times to make improvements to the program and to increase its usefulness to the farmers of Canada. Crop insurance was first sold to farmers in Manitoba in 1960 and the program was expanded to include Saskatchewan in 1961, Prince Edward Island in 1962, Alberta in 1965, Ontario in 1966, British Columbia in 1967, Quebec in 1968 and Nova Scotia in 1969.
Farmer participation has increased slowly and in 1972, the year just passed, 49,268 farmers purchased insurance worth $160 million, for a total premium of $11,172,000. Total indemnities which we expect will be paid on last year's insured crops will exceed $13 million, the largest crop losses occurring in Alberta, Ontario and Quebec.
I have said the number of farmers protected by crop insurance in 1972 was 49,000. This represents less than 20 per cent of the number of farmers who are eligible to purchase this protection. There are, I believe, several reasons why many farmers have not used this program, and Bill C-129 before the House is one major step toward meeting farmers' objections, particularly the objection that the level of the guarantee is too low and the premium is too high.
Variation in crop yields is one of the major risks of farming. This variation can be caused by a number of unavoidable actions of nature. The cost of any insurance program that might be designed to compensate a farmer for any crop damage would be prohibitive. Therefore, crop insurance is a program to guarantee a level of production on a farmer's total crop up to 80 per cent of a farmer's previous average yield, so that when a crop is seriously reduced the farmer is assured of a return which will generally cover his investment in the crop. While many farmers prefer the higher guarantee, the premium cost is often prohibitive when added to all the costs that a farmer faces each spring of the year. The most common level of coverage is 60 to 70 per cent of average yield, and the average premium for this coverage has exceeded 7 per cent.
In the 12 years that crop insurance has been sold in Canada, $73,187,000 has been collected in premiums, of which the farmers have paid $52,643,011, and $70,800,000 has been paid to farmers whose crops were less than the guarantee. Thus, for each premium dollar paid by farmers in total, farmers in total have received $1.35. Each year improvements are made in the terms and conditions of crop insurance plans to meet farmers' needs, but this bill will be a big step in permitting improvements in the size of the guarantee in relation to the cost to the farmer.
I expect that the number of farmers who buy crop insurance in the next few years will nearly double. The basic idea of crop insurance, that a farmer decides to purchase protection before he sows a crop, is new to many farmers. Many farmers continue to self-insure, to take a chance, to diversify to reduce risk of crop loss, or to rely on government emergency grants. My experience of this sort of thing is not good. All it amounts to is a lot of buck-passing between the two higher levels of govern-

March 29, 1973
Crop Insurance Act
ment and the farmer generally ends up holding the empty bucket.
As all provinces step up their efforts to explain the advantages and operation of crop insurance, and particularly with the ever increasing need for higher cash investment in every crop, I can see the majority of farmers using this program in the near future and benefiting from the stability of income that it provides.
I might add that since being appointed Minister of Agriculture I have visited and consulted every one of my provincial counterparts and discussed the changes that we think are desirable in crop insurance for Canadian farmers. I am still receiving suggestions from them. I have done the same thing with all the farm organizations. I have attended many public farm meetings and asked farmers to suggest the changes that they think would be practical to make crop insurance more enticing to the agricultural industry as a whole.
At the first federal-provincial meeting of agricultural ministers this has top place on our agenda, so that new and even better legislation than that which is on the books will be presented to farmers in the crop year 1974-75. Crop insurance, I think, is something they all want. They want an insurance plan that is closer to their idea of what real insurance should be, that is closer to the principle of insurance as we all know it.
I might also add that I know a bit about insurance since I sold casualty insurance part-time for seven and a half years and was director of Co-operators Insurance, the largest casualty insurance company in Ontario. I must say that I think our crop insurance program has a long way to go before it is what many producers and farmers in this nation want it to be, that is, real insurance that guarantees them against loss. I am willing to listen to any reasonable presentation by any member of this House, by any group or by any one of my provincial counterparts, so that we have the most advanced and progressive type of crop insurance in the world.

subsubtopic: REIMBURSEMENT TO PROVINCES FOR PARTIAL ADVANCES ON CROP INSURANCE PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has taken this opportunity to introduce an amendment to the Crop Insurance Act. Crop insurance is a prime topic among farmers today due, I think, to the terrible experience that farmers in various provinces have had because of weather, flood conditions and so on, all of them acts of God. Not only were farmers unable to cope with these disasters and prevent the tremendous damage that was caused, but farmers found themselves in most instances unable to cope with them financially.
When one thinks of crop insurance from the farmer's point of view, he thinks of an investment in the form of a premium to safeguard against partial or total crop loss which might place the farmer in an economic strait-jacket as far as financing further crops or other farming activities is concerned.
We have had the matter of crop insurance before us for a number of years. As an indication of the fact that something is drastically wrong, let me point out that in 1972, of the hundreds of thousands of farmers in Canada

who could take out crop insurance only 46,000 availed themselves of this opportunity. This was a decrease of almost 7,000 farmers from the 1970-71 crop year. This would lead one to believe that the farmers are not satisfied with the present crop insurance plan. They are discouraged to the extent they are not taking advantage of the minor provision available to them at the present time.
What is the basic problem? When you talk to farmers, as most of us have, who have experienced flood, hail, rain, wind or fire damage, you will find that farmers are very blunt. You ask them why they do not take out crop insurance and nine out of ten will say quite bluntly, "Because it is not worth a damn." That is their attitude. I think you will find that their experience has not been happy in respect of crop insurance. You cannot point the finger of blame at any one segment of government or any particular administration.
One of the basic problems which we face is related to the structure of crop insurance. It is initiated by the federal government and administered by the provincial governments in ten different ways; they are not universal in their application or methods. When you have a situation like this you are bound to have disruption, time lapses and maladministration, all of which leads to dissatisfaction.
The minister stated-I was happy to hear this-that the government is going to try to initiate coverage up to 80 per cent of loss. This sounds reasonable on the face of it, but in the actual application so far as the farmer is concerned, it does not work out that way. A farmer may have one field, part of which is on a slope and part of which is on the level; one part may be along a river flat and one part on an incline. Part of this field may suffer 40 per cent crop damage, while the other part is not damaged at all. When this happens the farmer is not eligible for any compensation because in total he has lost only 20 per cent of his crop. This is just one example; there are many.
The decision as to whether a farmer is eligible for compensation is a human one. Let us consider a crop of tomato plants, potato plants or tobacco plants. Such a crop, when hit by hail or a rain deluge, suffers a great deal of damage. The plants sit in water for a week or so and the roots are killed because of lack of oxygen. An inspector comes in to assess the damage. His assessment is never in accord with the damage the farmer believes he has suffered; the farmer feels he has suffered much greater loss than the inspector is willing to admit. We have many instances of crop loss which work severe economic hardship on the farmers involved, yet under the administration of the crop insurance plan they receive absolutely no payment. This is why farmers have lost faith in this particular type of coverage.
I know the minister was earnest and sincere when he said he was willing to hear suggested improvements. He has travelled across the country and talked to provincial ministers of agriculture, and I know he appreciates the difficulties. I am delighted that this bill is to be sent to committee where we can call witnesses and study it in detail, following which we can draw our own conclusions. There is no objection on the part of this party to sending the bill to committee. We believe crop insurance is an absolute necessity for farmers of this nation.
March 29, 1973

Under the economic situation which faces Canada today, farming is not a simple operation; it is a very complicated and high-investment industry. When this industry was new, $400 would buy all the machinery and equipment necessary to operate a 150-acre farm. But $400 today would hardly pay for the forms of energy required to turn over the machinery on the average farm for a week. That is the problem we face today. When we speak about farming today, we are not speaking about a $3,000 or $5,000 investment; in many instances we are speaking about an investment of $250,000 to $1.5 million. The operators of farms are interested in crop insurance to protect their investment.
We must not approach this matter on the basis of a simple bill relating to a primary industry, but as a measure for the protection of a very complicated business enterprise. Unless this crop insurance program is a businesslike proposition, the farmers will not be interested in it. It is our experience over the past number of years that they are not interested; this is borne out by the small number of farmers who have availed themselves of the plan.
Some 46,000 farmers have taken out crop insurance,
13,000	of whom are located in the western provinces, the birthplace of crop insurance. Therefore the House can understand the hesitation of farmers to participate in this program in other provinces. This is why we look forward to getting the bill before the committee, at which time members of this party will have suggestions to make and perhaps will move some amendments.
Let me go back to the principle I dealt with a moment ago in respect of differences in administration. Today the minister put forward a simple proposition to increase the federal contribution to the administrative costs of the program in an attempt to lower farmers' premiums. The idea is that if a farmer has to pay $1 an acre for a very simple crop insurance plan, the government will pick up, depending upon the province involved, 25 per cent or 50 per cent of the premium.
This is not the only type of insurance required by farmers. When we speak about crop insurance we cannot confine ourselves to small payments for a portion of a crop which may not be harvested. Such an approach has proved to be very unsatisfactory in respect of some segments of farming. If hon. members wish specifics, I will be specific and speak on behalf of the dairy farmers or those who produce beef. It is very difficult to compensate such a producer "X" number of dollars an acre for the amount of hay he was unable to take in because of a deluge of rain.
When such a disaster occurs, it affects not only one farmer but his neighbours in the next concession, those in the next township and often those in the next country. So we have an entire area that has lost the necessary forage. When you compensate the farmer by "X" number of dollars per acre on the basis of the hay he did not take in, you are only paying him on the basis of normal production. When we have a disaster such as this, the farmer is forced to pay for forage at a price which is sometimes tremendously high, not only because of an increase due to scarcity of supply but often due to the necessity to truck forage or take it by rail hundreds of miles into the area. All these
Crop Insurance Act
things add to the cost, and the only avenue available to farmers is through supplication to the Minister of Agriculture and the federal government for extra grants and loans to take care of the situation.
Is it not more logical or sensible, when we are setting up a crop insurance program, to design it to provide most benefit to farmers? Farmers to whom I have spoken across this nation-I, too, have been across this nation-are not too concerned about the actual insurance premium per acre. Certainly they do not want to pay more than they must pay, but they are not too concerned about the degree of premium, that is, whether it be $1, $1.50 or $2 per acre. They are more interested in what it will buy if they should be faced with a catastrophe. They are more concerned about whether it will help them in the event of flooding of their entire crop, destruction by hail, by early or late frost, or by fire. This is what farmers are interested in.
However, unfortunately it seems that the total emphasis of the government continues to be on providing an extra 25 per cent of the premium per acre or in helping the provincial governments in respect of their .administrative costs. It is all right for the minister to tell the House, which either he or his parliamentary secretary probably will, that the administration of these policies comes under provincial jurisdiction and that the province works out the actual mechanics of crop insurance. This no doubt is true, but the fact remains that there is a federal responsibility in the entire scheme. It seems to me the onus is on the government, through the Minister of Agriculture, to work out with the ministers of agriculture of the provinces a plausible, practical, logical crop insurance program which would be universal to the degree that it would be attractive to farmers, that they would have confidence in it and would feel their desires were met.
I am not impressed by the argument of the minister tonight when he told us that for every dollar in the form of premium which farmers invest in crop insurance, they receive $1.30. I am not impressed because many farmers who would receive $1.30 are today working in the towns and cities because they went bankrupt on the farm. They are there because disaster broke their economic backs. This is why we must look at this problem in a little different light. If the federal government is sincere in its plans to develop a viable, economic agricultural industry in this country, it must consider long-range plans.
First of all, this government must decide whether it believes an agricultural industry in Canada is indispensable. Never on this side of the House have we been able to determine, from the actions of the government, whether it feels this industry is indispensable. If the government believes it is, then it is time it started a long-range policy designed to put the business of agriculture on the basis on which it is entitled to be. When I speak of it being on a business basis, this is what I have in mind. All the farmers of this nation wish for an economic climate, not in which they need subsidies, not in which they need hand-outs or small loans from the governments at low interest rates, not all these tools for cripples but, rather, an economic climate in which they can receive the same return for their labour and capital investment as that received by all

March 29, 1973
Crop Insurance Act
other segments of the Canadian economy. If they get this, they will be satisfied.
We have an opportunity tonight, through this bill, to take one of the first steps in changing the policy and directing it so that the farmers will know that the Parliament of Canada feels their industry is absolutely necessary and that we are starting to take steps to make it possible for them to survive under the really tough international competition with which they are faced. The way to do it is by starting to lay the basis of an insurance plan that will give them some confidence in their own longterm investments, so that they do not have the absolute dread that one disaster, one act of God, in one year could wipe them out of business.
When we have succeeded in doing this-and I think we can-when we have established an insurance policy for Canadian farmers all across Canada which will fully compensate them for complete crop failure due to an act of God, then this parliament will have begun to do something worth while for the farmers of this nation.

subsubtopic: REIMBURSEMENT TO PROVINCES FOR PARTIAL ADVANCES ON CROP INSURANCE PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unless I am mistaken, I think this is the first bill amending an act which has been introduced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I congratulate him on taking some action in respect of the crop insurance legislation. Part of the question-this was touched on by the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Danforth) who spoke immediately before me-is whether the changes proposed by the minister will make this program really operative and one that will attract farmers to use it and have the protection they need. I wonder if it will.
We know the experience up to 1971-72. I am referring to the 1971-72 annual report in respect of crop insurance. It states that 46,326 farmers in Canada purchased crop insurance in 1971, and this was 13 per cent fewer than in
1970.	So actually crop insurance has been attracting fewer farmers as time goes by. I do not have the figures here for Manitoba, but I have talked to some of the people in that province. Manitoba really tried to use crop insurance, but I think participation in the program is starting to decline.
In this bill the government proposes to increase to some extent the amount of money which it will pay. It will pay up to 50 per cent of the premium and the provinces will cover the administration costs. These are the essential features of the bill. Again I ask: Will this be sufficient to attract the vast majority of farmers into taking out this kind of insurance and paying the premiums? I have spoken to people in my constituency in Saskatchewan. I spoke to a man who is actively selling insurance to farmers in the area. There is a real drive to get farmers to take out crop insurance. If they had coverage, it would be protection against some of the disasters that we have experienced this year.
I would have liked to learn from the minister whether as a result of these new proposals he was expecting to absolve the government from responsibility to meet the kinds of disasters that occurred this year in Ontario, Quebec and the Peace River area of Alberta and British Columbia. I still have my doubts that this type of insur-

ance will be able to compensate for those kinds of disasters, especially if farmers encounter a situation where they suffer drought or flooding for two or three years in succession. Is it the government's belief that, having enacted this kind of crop insurance, it can opt out of giving special assistance in such cases? I think it is taking the wrong attitude, if it believes so. Individualized insurance such as this will not cope with those situations.
I was interested to hear the minister say he wanted to get this scheme on a straight insurance basis. He said that he had sold insurance and that this was the way he was thinking. I am convinced that ordinary, straight-ahead individual insurance will prove to be the answer for the farmers. Some years ago I hoped that in western Canada some minister or some government would be imaginative enough to try to tie in PFAA with a crop insurance program. It could have worked in the three prairie provinces at least. One could take the major crops and make a deduction, at the same time use the individual insurance approach, and by amalgamating the two achieve over-all coverage. It would mean collecting premiums from the farmers. From the deductions you could build up a fund of considerable magnitude which would cope with a disaster when it occurred.
I am sorry to see the principle behind PFAA, which was to make a deduction right across the board in order to provide protection right across the board, being written off in order to go back-the minister may say, go forward-to a simple, straight insurance scheme where each farmer carries his own risk, with a certain amount of contribution for the premium being paid by the federal government or the provincial government as the case may be.
I think it will take some time before we get the vast majority of farmers covered under the scheme as it is now established. Some years ago I went to a meeting in my municipality which was attended by farmers from all around the area. The local ag rep attended, and we discussed this idea at length. We asked the farmers whether they would buy insurance to get this kind of coverage. The answer we received was that they would not. I would point out that the area around Rosetown and Biggar is representative of the central grain growing region of western Canada. If the crop insurance scheme is to be successful, it must appeal to that type of farmer.
The minister says he has gone across the country and spoken to farmers and to governments. I wonder if he really thinks that the farmers in Kindersley, Alsask, Medicine Hat, Maple Creek, Swift Current and all through that area, who farm one or two, or even four or five sections will use this program; or does he think there will still be a significant number of farmers in certain categories who will not use it? This is the question that needs to be answered, because most people would agree that if an insurance program is to be effective it must be universal.
I have my doubts whether the legislation that will emerge as a result of these amendments will achieve that objective. But we will have to wait only three or four years to find the answer. Instead of covering 46,326 farmers, if the scheme that is proposed tonight really is the answer it will cover 300,000 to 400,000 farmers. Does the minister expect this to happen? Quite frankly, I doubt
March 29, 1973

that it will. I do not particularly want to run down the idea, but if we are to have a program, it had better work and we must have good reason to believe that it will.
As I say, there is no special provision for disaster years; or at least the minister has not said there is. I think I am being fair when I say that his predecessor gave a clear indication that his objective was to establish policies which meant we would no longer have to ask the federal government for special assistance for the farmers. I believe that the amendment to the Crop Insurance Act was meant to achieve that major objective. That thread runs through the policies which this government and the one before it have proposed to the House. It ran through the policies in connection with the grains stabilization bill, that is, to have the government move out of any special category and adopt an automatic program that would meet the farmers' needs when incomes dropped.
As well as crop insurance we should look at the income policies of the government. After all, this kind of insurance is meant to maintain income in years of disaster. Over-all income is what the government should be concerned with. As well as this, we should be talking about changes to the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Either deliberately or by accident, some of the policies that we thought would be fairly effective-and were at one time- have become ineffective. I think part of it has happened by design. The Agricultural Prices Support Act has a ten-year average for the main basis of support, and 80 per cent of that is offered to farmers as a support price. Surely the minister and the government know that this act is largely inoperative because of the rise in prices. Just take the example of pork. When the price of hogs went down to $19 and $20 a hundredweight, the amount provided in the act was so low that for shame they dared not offer it to the farmers; they had to use an arbitrary figure, a large figure. How long is the government content to leave this situation as it is?
In his speech the minister said there might be some suggestions from this side. I suggest that he can start by shortening that ten-year average to five year, and by changing the 80 per cent to 100 per cent. He should then get somebody with a slide-rule to find out what the figures show. They might show a price support program that would be worth having on the statute books. Sheep men have come here time after time in the last three years and pleaded with the government for help in this regard.
The farmer is logical enough that he will not pay for insurance unless it will guarantee him an income on which he can live. One of the major reasons the insurance program did not grow, and instead declined in Saskatchewan and Manitoba through 1969, 1970 and 1971, was that the farmer's income was so low that it was not worth insuring, and he could not afford to insure it. The minister knows that; it is in this report. It does nothing for the farmer to offer a program to insure an income which in a year or two from now may not be worth insuring.
I have listened to the minister when he has spoken before the food committee, and I have read some of the speeches he has made across the country. He tells consumers that the farmer is giving them bargains. He is
Crop Insurance Act
right; this government has helped the farmer to give bargains. The program which he proposes tonight assumes that there will not be disaster years. Of course, disasters are not the minister's fault but if there is not an agricultural prices support program to protect the farmer, it will be his fault; he will be responsible and should be called to account in this House. I see no sign that the government intends to deal with this matter. I see signs that they are proposing to let supply and demand make the decisions in the market.
The minister in charge of the Wheat Board says he is interested in farm income, although he never says what kind or at what level. Someone asked what he is going to do about putting rapeseed under the Wheat Board, and he said: Maybe this year, next year, come day, go day, God send Sunday; I am going to do something-maybe. He comes to this House and tells farmers what is the initial price for barley and wheat, and that he would like them to grow more rapeseed, too; but he does not offer any kind of support or price for rapeseed. Again, the farmer is to take the whole risk; he is to insure a crop when he has no guarantee of its value and no support against a disaster price. He just has to take his chance.
The same minister says he will keep supplying wheat to the millers at $1,951. Even the farmers of Ontario are starting to plead with him to have the millers pay what the wheat is worth, because this is denying them a fair price for their product. Nothing is being done about it. This is the second time this sort of thing has happened; the first time was during the Second World War. Why not take the necessary action to increase the price of wheat to millers? Speaking of that portion of the wheat payments which comes from the treasury, the minister responsible for the *Wheat Board said it is "clearly a consumer subsidy holding the price of bread down instead of letting it reflect world prices for wheat." This must be the biggest laugh in the world. Tell that to the consumers. Tell them the price of bread is held down. Somebody should go through the country and tell the people that, so they will know. That is the kind of irrationality we have been fed from time to time.
Speaking to the bill before us, I am in favour of developing crop insurance protection that the farmer can purchase and that will protect him against flood, hail, drought, and so on. Let me say to the minister, however, that this will only work and be accepted by farmers if they are given the opportunity to realize an income that is adequate for their needs. If farmers find themselves in the position of obtaining an adequate income, they will not run to the minister or anybody else looking for hand-outs: they will carry all the insurance they need and will look after themselves. We do not yet have policies that would place farmers in that position. Let me leave this thought with the minister: if he wants this program to work, he must acquire a better grasp of the situation and look at it in a broader context than he has until now.

subsubtopic: REIMBURSEMENT TO PROVINCES FOR PARTIAL ADVANCES ON CROP INSURANCE PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say a few words about the suggestions of the

March 29, 1973
Crop Insurance Act
government, and especially on Bill C-129 the purpose of which is to give the farmers better crop insurance.
For a few years now, that insurance has certainly helped the farmers, but all are not insured; several were, but when time came for them to claim insurance benefits, they had a very hard time getting their losses assessed.
I know the inspection must be made in co-operation with the provincial governments; I also know that everything does not depend on the federal government, but I ask the minister whether he could-or perhaps has he done so already-consult with the provinces that a body might be appointed in each one to inspect the damages and so enable the farmers to collect their insurance.
In fact, a number of farmers suffered substantial losses and were unable to collect insurance because the damages to their crops could not be evaluated. It often happened that they called on inspectors in due time to look at the crops and the inspectors came around three months later, right in the middle of winter, which is certainly not the right time to evaluate crops. It was therefore decided that a number of farmers could not collect insurance, for the reasons I have given.
I agree with the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) when he says the insurance did not fulfill the required purpose. In my riding, which is semi-rural and semi-urban, a number of farmers declined to take advantage of the insurance. About 25 per cent did use the plan. I wonder why farmers did not take advantage of this insurance. Probably because they thought it did not offer enough advantages or because inspections are not made on schedule when damages are to be assessed. At any rate, only 25 per cent of farmers are insured and 75 per cent are not.
During last summer or fall, because of large losses in crops, caused by too much rain, the government decided to grant $400 to each farmer to help with the damages. About half my constituency was declared a designated area whereas the other half had the same damages and could not obtain these benefits because it was not designated as such.
In the course of the election campaign, this became a political argument and it was said that one area of the constituency was not recognized as designated because of its member sitting in the opposition. Yet, in the other part of the constituency, each farmer was granted $400 because it had been recognized as a designated area.
Mr. Speaker, there is certainly something the matter with this situation. I suggest it is unreasonable to do such things in a constituency. I don't know whether this has occurred elsewhere-I have not inquired, I have not pushed the matter further. In any case, this is what happened.
The $400 grant benefited to some, but others who incurred losses of more than $6,000 received only $400. There is again something that is not entirely fair in this. Many farmers are still dissatisfied that they received only $400, whereas they incurred much heavier losses. So, there is some injustice in this.
The initiative of giving $400 to farmers who suffered rain damage is contrary to the principle of crop insurance. This does not encourage farmers to buy more insur-
(Mr. Latulippe.]
ance, because probably they think that if they suffer damage, they need not pay insurance premiums because the government will subsidize damaged crops.
I think, moreover, that the minister should intercede with the provincial authorities so as to clear up this matter. There is definitely something unfair about the present insurance plan, which in no way solves the problem. Under the proposed insurance plan, the federal government undertakes responsibility for half of the insured parties and pays 50 per cent of the premiums, which I am not opposed to.
We shall definitely support this bill, although it will not directly solve the farmers' problems. It is a pretty lame sort of aid, as the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar said just now.
It is true that the provinces are the ones who decide; so the ministers of agriculture of all the provinces ought to negotiate clear agreements with the federal government. What is needed is insurance that would really cover crops that were ruined; if there were such a crop insurance plan, the government would not be obliged, as it has been in the past, to pay out $400 subsidies to help farmers whose crops have been damaged.
And so we need to set up a crop insurance plan that would really be of help to Canadian agriculture; if we did, I think all farmers would want coverage. Something must be wrong if only 25 per cent of farmers buy insurance.
I am no expert on insurance, but I know that there is something wrong since farmers are hesitant about insuring their crops.
As to the establishment of insurance policies, they should really insure crops, and when damage occurs, there should be an organization ready to take the proper steps and inspect where needed so that our farmers could benefit from this insurance which must insure and not only appear to. It should not be an insurance that does not pay when it is time to pay. When damages suffered by farmers must be paid for, this should be done quickly. This organization should operate in such a way that our farmers could really benefit from it and would be truly insured in an adequate manner.
I also doubt that this bill will be satisfactory to the great majority of farmers. I do not think there are that many changes in this bill. The bill should have been better explained. It should be referred to committee for a more thorough examination by agricultural experts who would give their views and bring valid solutions to allow our farmers to really benefit from crop insurance.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leopold Corriveau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: REIMBURSEMENT TO PROVINCES FOR PARTIAL ADVANCES ON CROP INSURANCE PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased this evening to speak about Bill C-129 because it shows that the present government and especially the Department of Agriculture, through the minister, are trying once again to give all Canadian farmers a tool enabling them to live comfortably and above all in security on their land.
As the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Latulippe) pointed out just now, last year in Quebec-I refer to Quebec because I am a member of that province-some weather
March 29, 1973

problems have inflicted rather heavy losses to farmers. Unfortunately, most of those farmers were not covered by crop insurance, which means that very few were insured.
Thanks to this bill, all Canadian farmers will be happy to find out that the government intends to give them a coverage which will enable them to remain on the farm when facing problems such as those that occurred last year.
Bill C-129 provides for another way of cost sharing between the federal government, the provinces and the farmers. Pursuant to this legislation, the contributions of the federal government, under the terms of a federal-provincial agreement, may reach up to 50 per cent of the total premiums, provided the province pays for all administrative costs. The producers' share would be 50 per cent of the premium. The federal contribution provided for in the bill would be paid by way of refund to the provincial government for the amount paid into the crop insurance fund of each province.
In 1972-73, the farmers of Nova Scotia, Quebec and Ontario have taken out crop insurance by paying 50 per cent of the premium. In the other provinces where crop insurance schemes are in force, the farmers had to pay 75 per cent of the premium. The cost sharing arrangements provided for in Bill C-129 will allow all Canadian farmers to take out crop insurance by paying 50 per cent of the premium.
Greater federal participation will result in more crop protection at a lesser cost per acre to the farmer. In addition, with the experience gained by the provincial administrations, the protection offered the farmer by guaranteeing that his crop is protected, will be of considerable value to all Canadian farmers.
Mr. Speaker, I trust all hon. members will support this bill which will give every Canadian farmer more security.
Crop insurance schemes have evolved somewhat. The Crop Insurance Act was passed by the federal government in 1959. Afterwards, it was applied in 1960 on a trial basis in Manitoba. Since then, eight provinces have provided crop insurance programs for farmers, namely Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Prince Edward Island, Alberta, Ontario, British Columbia, Quebec and Nova Scotia.
Initially the Crop Insurance Act entitled the federal government to enter into agreements with the provinces and to assume 50 per cent of the administrative costs and 20 per cent of the necessary premiums to apply the insurance. It also included provisions enabling the federal government to make loans to the provinces in the years when compensation requests would by far exceed the available reserves to indemnify the claimants.
Amendments have been made to the 1959 act in 1964, 1966 and 1971. The amendments of 1964 did away with loans and the federal government agreed to reinsure part of the risk incurred by the provinces, through an approved crop insurance plan. Then, when provinces decided to join the crop insurance plan, the federal government was willing to do something in this area.
Services offered through crop insurance are numerous. As a matter of fact, services offered by the Department of Agriculture of Canada under the Crop Insurance Act include assistance to provinces in order to promote,
Crop Insurance Act
improve and change their crop insurance plan; the central co-ordination of programs designed to improve and further expand the insurance of crop losses for Canadian farmers; studies aimed at setting crop insurance plans on sound actuarial footings, and the carrying out of financial commitments involved in cost sharing agreements between the Federal government and the Provinces, as regards the share of premium and administration costs as well as the reinsurance of risk.
In 1971, crops have not been too good in most regions of Canada. Important crop losses were recorded in some regions of Canada, for various causes. In Quebec as in other provinces, bad weather during the sowing season or during crops was responsible for farmers losing considerable amounts of money. As we know the problems of farmers who suffer such important losses, we must support this new bill on crop insurance in order to help them.
The financial contributions of the federal Department of Agriculture to the crop insurance program cover the administration costs of the crop insurance division as well as payment made under the agreements between the federal and provincial governments. The Department of Insurance also offers at no cost continuing advisory services.
If indemnities to be paid exceed premiums collected, funds are advanced by provincial governments or under federal provincial insurance agreements.
The administrators of the crop insurance program are continuously trying to improve the provisions of crop insurance contracts to meet the needs of farmers in various areas. However, it seems administration should be improved so a larger proportion of farmers will understand the program and feel confident enough about it to use it regularly.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should all try to make farmers understand that crop insurance is really intended to help them survive periods as dead as those we knew last year and to prevent the same problems from re-occurring.
Mr. Speaker, it gave me great pleasure to say a few words tonight on Bill C-129 designed to help the farmers of Canada.

subsubtopic: REIMBURSEMENT TO PROVINCES FOR PARTIAL ADVANCES ON CROP INSURANCE PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on the crop insurance bill. I wish the minister well with regard to it. It is a small step in the right direction. I have to say, though, that it is late. In my area of Saskatchewan crops are already being seeded and the government of the province has not seen fit to offer lower premium rates to producers. So the sign-up out there is slow.
It seems to me the changes proposed in this bill are administrative rather than anything else. Looking over the annual report on crop insurance, I see there are 18 administrative costs to be borne by the insured farmer, which amounted to 18 per cent of the premium in Saskatchewan in the last three years. It makes one wonder. Really, the amount of money involved, $4 million last year, is so small in relation to the value of the industry as to make the plan almost worthless.

March 29, 1973
Crop Insurance Act
The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) suggested that crop insurance and PFAA might have been put together. That is a very sensible idea. Surely we need an agricultural insurance policy which covers a farmer's total income, which includes livestock enterprises as well as crops. The sign-up on the Prairies has been very slow for crop insurance, particularly in the province of Saskatchewan. The reason, of course, is that in the spring we are asking farmers to pay a stiff premium. On 200 acres, in the area I represent, the premium is about $476, and on 400 acres it is around $1,000. Admittedly, the government is proposing to take up half of this charge, but the remainder is still a lot of money to ask the farmer to lay out before he seeds a crop.
I should like to deal for a few minutes with the industry we are insuring. Canada is the second largest country in the world and we are rich in resources and opportunities. Yet the policies of the federal Department of Agriculture in the last few years have been inward-looking. We have become preoccupied with regional squabbles. In the west, we realize that our problems and our priorities are not the same as those of other regions of Canada. We know that steps must be taken to equalize standards and opportunities across this land; so once again I welcome this bill.
Our main crop in western Canada is wheat. Only two other countries in the world grow the hard, red spring wheat that we do-the United States, in its northern part, and Australia. We are the only three countries which grow this bread-making wheat for export. No other grain can be substituted for this wheat. This wheat can only be grown to best advantage in semi-arid conditions. This makes us extremely vulnerable to the whims of mother nature. So the Government of Canada has a real responsibility to help protect this wealth-producing industry. We have to carry over a large stock at the end of each crop year in order to be classed as a dependable supplier by the rest of the world.
The importance of grain to the Canadian economy can be considered in a number of ways. The commonest way is to take account of the direct contribution of grain sales to farm income and the amount added to the gross national wealth. But a more revealing way is to take account of the economic activity generated by wheat sales in various industrial sectors, since so many jobs and enterprises depend, direct or indirectly, on agricultural output. The production, distribution and export of 600 million bushels of wheat at the present price of $2.75 a bushel-which amounts to $1.4 billion-generates a total domestic output of $4.4 billion. The Agricultural Economic Research Council has all the figures. Total government revenue from the 600 million bushels exported amounts to $675 million. So the effect generated on the economy corresponds to $4.4 billion, direct income amounts to $2.1 billion and $675 million goes to the federal government. And I would remind hon. members that important though these exports are, western production of other grains used for processing, and so on, has an even more important effect upon the economy. It is now obvious it would have been possible to have sold, at competitive world prices, the production from 10 million acres removed by the government's Lift program. This was a direct loss to the Canadian economy of over $500 million, and to the food system of over $700 million.

We can turn the question around and ask, what could the government afford to pay in the way of market development, export assistance or price subsidization and be no worse off? Several partial analyses have revealed that a government promotion of $1 per bushel could be provided for wheat, and this would result in direct and indirect benefits accruing to all sectors of the Canadian economy. I suggest that the federal government could well afford to be more generous than they have been in the provisions of Bill C-129.
As I have said before, it is now a fact that Canada is a wealthy country. The financial resources of the federal treasury are such that if these moneys were redirected with a greater input toward agriculture, new concepts could be developed. Of primary importance is the realization that the producers in this country are entitled to a satisfactory return for their labour. In other words, they are entitled to prices to ensure their continuation in business and the accepted standard of life and opportunity Canada affords. If the marketplace cannot provide these requirements, then it is my contention that Canada should.
Agriculture is a permanent foundation for economic activity, as contrasted with resource-depleting industries. One thing is important to keep in mind, however. Whatever is done must not be done at the expense of soil deterioration. The land should not be overworked in order to compensate for excessive grain shortages, nor should it be considered worthless in times of overproduction. Our main objective has to be to increase food output. Food is so basic a commodity and so necessary that the federal government must be involved. In effect, only three areas of the world produce more than they consume-Canada, the United States and the European Common Market. New prosperity around the world and new political realities ensure demand for better food.
It is said, Mr. Speaker, that a journey of 1,000 miles starts with a single step. I think this is a single step that we are taking tonight, and I look forward to dealing further with the bill when it reaches the committee.

subsubtopic: REIMBURSEMENT TO PROVINCES FOR PARTIAL ADVANCES ON CROP INSURANCE PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not take too long tonight so we can get this bill through second reading as quickly as possible. I should like, first of all, to say on behalf of my party that we welcome the bill. We feel it is a step in the right direction. At the present time, farmers in my province have been subsidized to the tune of 25 per cent of their premium for crop insurance. Now they will be getting 50 per cent of their premium through the auspices of the federal government.
One thing that does bother me is this. In my province, in fact in the prairie provinces, there was a decrease in participation in the crop insurance plan during the crop year 1971-1972. In Saskatchewan and Alberta I suppose we could put part of the blame on Lift, the Lower Inventory for Tomorrow program-or, as some people in Saskatchewan call it, "lower income for tomorrow"-and the grasslands incentive program.
Saskatchewan has the largest cultivated acreage in Canada. According to a report that I received some time ago, we have the third highest insured acreage. One
March 29, 1973

matter that the committee on agriculture will have to delve into very seriously is how we can get more farmers involved in crop insurance. I suppose we will have to convince the farmers that crop insurance is good for them, and make it so attractive that all of them will want to participate.
This report, the annual report of the minister under the Crop Insurance Act for 1971-72, is not completely up to date since we are now in 1973, but I should like to put on the record what measures have been taken in my home province to extend the crop insurance scheme. What the provincial government of Saskatchewan is doing, together with the proposed amendment in this bill to the Crop Insurance Act, should make crop insurance more worth while for Saskatchewan farmers.
To begin with, in the early phases of crop insurance in Saskatchewan, which commenced in the early 1960s, not too much progress was made during the seven Liberal years that we had. There was a Tory-Grit coalition to keep us out of power. But then we managed to get back in. Since 1971, crop insurance has been extended to include all agricultural areas of the province. Originally it covered only the eastern section of the province; now the entire province of Saskatchewan is covered.
The minister's report for 1971-72 indicates, on page 4, that in Saskatchewan the lands available before 1964 were for wheat, oats and barley only. I should like to inform the House that more crops have now been added and at the present time there are eight crops included under the crop insurance scheme in Saskatchewan. These are spring wheat, Durum wheat, barley, oats, fall rye, flax, sunflowers and rapeseed. Furthermore, coverages in general have been increased with inclusion of the latest yield data. A 70 per cent basic level of coverage is available for all crops included in the plan, in addition to the 60 per cent basic level of coverage. Also, a coverage adjustment feature which is based on individual crop insurance experience for insured crops is included.
A quality guarantee is included in addition to the quantity guarantee, and provides that if production is reduced in quality due to an insured hazard, the grade is also considered in determining the loss in production. Hail losses will also be adjusted on an individual field and on a spot loss basis. This provides protection against partial losses through hail and at the same time maintains an over-all guarantee as provided under the basic crop insurance plan.
In addition, an expanded program of information and promotion is being carried out. This is something the federal government could be doing. We must have a change in the method of selling and servicing so that more farmers in Saskatchewan are involved. In my constituency, and I live in the fringe area of agricultural land in Saskatchewan, about one-third of the farmers suffered heavy frost damage. Farmers who held crop insurance had an advantage over those who did not.
Since this is a federal-provincial program, I should like to indicate that the province of Saskatchewan is considering at the present time how it can better insure the farmer. In the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and
Crop Insurance Act
Manitoba, insurance is more or less based on the average yield for the last 25 years. One of the problems of determining whether a farmer should be insured on the basis of 5 per cent or 10 per cent of average yield is lack of statistics. At the present time, the government of Saskatchewan is trying to develop a system of establishing coverage for each insured based on the actual yields. This will require collecting yield data on an individual farm basis.
At the present time, risk area boundaries are based on municipal losses, which results in different rates of insurance on almost identical land and even within units. It would appear that rate areas should be segregated with land boundaries in respect of irrigation, soil and such things. It has also been contemplated that other crops should be insured under this new crop insurance scheme in addition to the eight I have already mentioned. One crop being contemplated is mustard seed.
A major concern of the farmers in Saskatchewan is that the crop insurance program by itself will not provide the production protection required if several consecutive disaster years should occur in a particular area. Since crop insurance guarantees only a portion of the long-term average yield, with present markets in respect of farming a farmer cannot survive at this level of production over a period of years. The increased contribution under the proposal should in no way relieve the Government of Canada from responsibility under adverse conditions such as I have mentioned. Once again, I feel that the crop insurance scheme has come a long way in Canada. It has made progress over the last 10 or 15 years, and I believe this is a step in the right direction. But we still have a long way to go.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in hearing what the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Corriveau) had to say when he suggested farmers would be proud of a government that brought in a crop insurance policy of this kind. Let me suggest that Ontario farmers are receiving virtually the same kind of deal this year, under this policy, that they received last year, and they will not find this acceptable. The hon. member is a long way out in left field in this regard, and if he continues to make statements like that he will find that he is not on the ball team at all.
The hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Nesdoly) said the government would be required to convince the farmers to buy insurance. I can only suggest that if he were acquainted with farmers he would know that you do not have to convince farmers about policies.

subsubtopic: REIMBURSEMENT TO PROVINCES FOR PARTIAL ADVANCES ON CROP INSURANCE PREMIUMS
speechtext: He is a farmer.

subsubtopic: REIMBURSEMENT TO PROVINCES FOR PARTIAL ADVANCES ON CROP INSURANCE PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Farmers know what they want, they know when they have a good deal and they will participate without being convinced.
I am pleased to participate in this debate on Bill C-129 because crop insurance is a matter of urgency. I had hoped the government would place before this House a crop insurance policy at an earlier date, in view of the fact that the fruit season in British Columbia commences on October 1, at which time there is danger of a first frost. Nevertheless, Bill C-129 must be considered and forward-
March 29, 1973

Crop Insurance Act
ed to the committee as quickly as possible. I would urge the government and the committee to accept reasonable and logical amendments such as those which have been suggested. No doubt there will be more. The minister has said he welcomes suggestions by members of this House, and I hope he will make use of them.
I realize the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has problems in attempting to have his proposals accepted by the cabinet. I hope he knew what he was talking about when he said he would accept the ideas of hon. members and use them when bringing forward new crop insurance legislation. Let me quote from the statement he made during the debate on the throne speech. As reported on page 344 of Hansard, the minister said:
These problems concerning crop insurance are hard to overcome. In view of these difficulties I believe it is time to re-examine the entire crop insurance program, to set out goals firmly in mind, and to develop a better program. During my trip across Canada, there was not one provincial minister of agriculture who did not bring this to my attention. They want the real principle of insurance embodied in crop insurance. They feel it is not in the program at the present time.
Again, I am open to suggestions from anyone who has any ideas on how we can improve the crop insurance program.
I wonder whether the Minister of Agriculture is disappointed with the results of his efforts as exemplified by Bill C-129, having made a statement of that magnitude? Although administrative costs are being shifted to provincial governments, with the federal government assuming responsibility for 50 per cent of the premiums, in most cases the farmer does not receive any greater protection. Bearing in mind the difficulties experienced by the minister in getting his point across to his colleagues, I wonder if he was forced to adopt a third official language which he now refers to as "Whelanese" in order to mesmerize the farmers into believing that his new policy would provide the answer to agricultural problems.

speechtext:
Being a new member, I find there is a great deal to learn about parliamentary rules and procedures. If we also need to learn "Whelanese" to properly understand the Minister of Agriculture, it will be an unexpected addition to the list of parliamentary rules and practices which every newly elected member is endeavouring to master.
In attempting to assess what the Minister of Agriculture has been saying, whether or not in "Whelanese", his phraseology has to be decoded. Once a person has the formula, or code, he has a better opportunity to understand what the minister means. For instance, when he spoke during the budget debate the minister said, as recorded at page 1580 of Hansard:
This is a budget for little people. They have benefited a great deal from the budget, more than others. Secondly, farmers will benefit from the changes made in the capital gains tax as it applies to transfers of farms from a father to the mother or child. This is a major concession, one that I am very happy to see in the budget.

What the minister is saying, in his third language, decoded, is that it was a stupid piece of legislation to begin with, which would eventually have destroyed the agricultural economy of this country; that the federal government admits that its inception was an error and is now trying to rescind the regulation. Actually, all that is being done is allowing transfer of a farm of a deceased to his wife, son or daughter without imposing the capital gains tax. In other words, a farmer, after labouring all his life to develop and maintain a farm for his own and his family's future, has to die to receive his just dues from this government. Apparently this is the way to say it in "Whelanese". Shakespeare put it more aptly, thus, "The good that men do is often interred with their bones".
To continue with the interpretation of "Whelanese" as shown on page 1248 of Hansard, when referring to fertilizer the minister said:
There is to be no price increase. The price will be the same as it was last August for all Alberta; it will not change in that area ... They have ample supplies ... At least that is one good bit of news, Mr. Chairman.
The truth of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, fertilizer is scarce and the situation will worsen, because many farmers do not have storage facilities, and therefore rely on its availability at seeding time to meet their needs. The price of fertilizer, quoted by one of the major retailers, if not the largest in Alberta, in January, 1972, for ammonium nitrate 34-0-0 was $63 per ton bulk. In January this year the same fertilizer cost $76 per ton. I want to stress the point that the minister either did not know what he was talking about, or he was deliberately trying to imply something which is not the truth, when he stated that the price of fertilizer in January would be the same as it was last August.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your guidance. I am guided by what you say, but I wanted to relate the cost of fertilizer and what the minister said to the bill with which we are dealing. Perhaps Your Honour would bear with me for a moment.
Those who purchase fertilizer know that the high price for the year is during July and August, and in the off-season during the months of September to January companies either lower prices generally or give a percentage discount. In the period to which I refer, the crop year 1970-71, there was a 7 per cent discount on fertilizer. During the 1972-73 crop year, the same company allowed a discount of 6 per cent. The minister ought to know that it is not honest to compare the reduced price in January to the high-season price of August. In addition, there has been an increase of $3 per ton right across the board for fertilizer. This is another example of "Whelanese" and of a government giving farmers and Canadians generally a false impression or a direct shafting.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, what has been said is a misinterpretation of the words I used. I said the information given to me was that if there were any
March 29, 1973

increase, it would be reasonable. I asked that if any member of this House had any information otherwise, he should bring it to my attention. subsubtopic: REIMBURSEMENT TO PROVINCES FOR PARTIAL ADVANCES ON CROP INSURANCE PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Each year, as the farmer's costs of production increase, crop insurance becomes more vital to his operation. Farmers must have a policy of crop insurance which is acceptable under present circumstances; a policy which is related to current problems; a policy of protection against partial or total crop loss; a policy that allows him to remain in production. If a farmer has the opportunity of participating in this type of crop insurance, he will purchase it. Last year only 18 to 24 per cent

this was mentioned by the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Dan-forth)-of those engaged in the production of food were able to afford crop insurance.
Something must be done to place crop insurance within financial reach so that every farmer can have its protection. Although the proposed legislation would be of benefit and will be supported by our party, if there is nothing better forthcoming we would like the minister to live up to his word by including suggested amendments to improve the crop insurance policy. I also hope the minister realizes it will take more than "Whelanese" to establish satisfactory crop insurance.
Last year in Canada the cost of production of agricultural products was approximately three times as much at it was 25 years ago, with grain selling at 10 per cent to 20 per cent less than during that period. These producers must be protected so that they can continue in business. If they do not lose their crops, they can survive. When their crops are destroyed and they do not have the protection of insurance, they are in serious trouble. When the crop insurance bill goes to committee, as was mentioned by my colleague the hon. member for Kent-Essex, we intend to propose an amendment in the hope that the government will accept it.
Some provinces are at present considering the implementation of a spot loss clause. I am convinced that crop insurance will never be a complete success unless this government permits the provinces to establish a spot loss policy on an acceptable maximum market value level above that established by the provincial governments on the basis of the market value of the crop. The federal government has failed to initiate proper leadership in the area of crop insurance. But if the Minister of Agriculture can convince his fellow cabinet members that inclusion of this type of plan into the formula which has been suggested in Bill C-129 is reasonable and practical, I believe it would be acceptable to the majority of farmers.
A successful crop insurance policy would help not only the farmer but every Canadian by their having an opportunity to buy food at lower prices. This would be an excellent way for a government to ensure that farmers are not forced out of production through crop loss. It is to the advantage of everyone to see that farmers continue in business if they so desire. Crop insurance most suitable for farmers can be provided through the federal govern-
Adjoumment Debate
ment working in co-operation with provincial governments. I would suggest that the Minister of Agriculture forget about trying to mislead the Canadian farmers. They are much too smart. What the farmers want is the truth and a crop insurance program that works.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-DISCUSSIONS ON AMENDMENT OF PENSION PLAN TO PROVIDE PAYMENTS ON BASIS OF 2 PER CENT PER YEAR OF SERVICE
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-DISCUSSIONS ON AMENDMENT OF PENSION PLAN TO PROVIDE PAYMENTS ON BASIS OF 2 PER CENT PER YEAR OF SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, January 15, 1973, as recorded in Hansard at page 275,1 asked this question:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Is the minister having discussions with Canadian National Railways concerning the desirability of amending the Canadian National pension plan to provide for pensions on the basis of 2 per cent for each year of service as is the case for Air Canada employees and federal public servants?
This was the reply of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand):
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific are now negotiating with the railway employees' unions and this is one of the items to be discussed. When I met the two presidents a few weeks ago, I indicated that I was certainly interested in the issue of the pension fund and I expressed hope that they would find a solution to this problem which has been pending too long already.
That was a good statement. The trouble is that "too long already" can go on until it becomes far too long. Subsequently, on Thursday, March 22, as recorded in Hansard at page 2489, I asked the Minister of Transport a question again on the same subject, using these words:

March 29, 1973
Adjournment Debate
Is the minister yet in a position to make a statement to the House concerning improvements in railway pensions, both Canadian National and Canadian Pacific? Also, can he tell the House whether he has been able to persuade Canadian National that its pensions should be at least equal to the pension provisions enjoyed by Air Canada employees and by employees of the federal public service?
The minister's answer was as follows:
I think the hon. gentleman knows that negotiations are presently going on between Canadian National, Canadian Pacific and the railway unions and that this subject is being discussed by the parties. I hope this very important problem of pensions will be solved this year, and I am ready to do whatever I can in order to obtain a just solution for the employees.
My purpose in rising tonight and recounting these two questions and answers is to express the hope that the minister is doing something in order to obtain a just solution of this problem. As some hon. members may be aware, reports have been leaking out to the effect that certain matters are being settled between the railway employees and the railway management. I do not have any definitive word as to what the terms of a possible settlement are. As a matter of fact, there is still a fair amount of confusion, but I am disturbed most of all over the fact that it seems some agreement is being reached with respect to the pension plans of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific, but that this agreement relates mainly, if not exclusively, to employees still working or, at best, with respect to very recent service.
One report that has come is that there will be pension improvements for those who were in service up to the end of 1972, and that an adjustment may go back as far as 1956. But for those who retired prior to 1956 on either railway there seems to be nothing in prospect so far as these reports are concerned.
Now, Mr. Speaker, because I have admitted that I do not know the details of any settlement that may be in prospect, it would not be proper for me to say much in that respect. However, 1 do want to impress upon the government, even though we are talking about something that is the subject of collective bargaining, that it has a responsibility to the employees of our major railways who are already retired.
Any settlement that is made that does not take into account the position of the older employees of Canada's railways should be reviewed by the government, and the government should do something about it. One of the railways is owned by the government, so surely the government can have some input into the question with that railway. I do not accept the argument so often advanced, that because the Canadian Pacific Railway is privately owned the government can do nothing about its pension plan. As a matter of fact, the Canadian Pacific lives in the public domain, has public support and has had a great deal of public money. I suggest that the federal government does have authority over that railway as well as over the Canadian National.
What is required in this area, Mr. Speaker, as a very minimum, is a pension plan that provides for a 2 per cent pension for each year of service that an employee has given to the railway. I believe a calculation along those lines should be made for employees already retired. There is also required a formula for the escalating of pensions, after retirement, better than the 2 per cent they now get

from the CNR. It should, in fact, be equal at least to the cost of living or, better still, to the rising standard of living.
There also needs to be an improvement in the position of widows of retired employees. At the present time, when a retired employee dies his widow gets a pension of only 50 per cent; most of us think it should be much more. There also should be provision for early retirement without severe penalty, as is now the case.
These are the things that ought to be enshrined in railway pensions. They ought to be at least as good as the best provisions there are for Air Canada and federal public servants. As a matter of fact, I would like to see their pensions as good as pensions provided for members of the House of Commons.
My plea to the government tonight is to recognize the fact that even though this subject is being dealt with at the collective bargaining table, the government has a special responsibility to those already retired. I hope this year will not go by without something substantial and meaningful being done for all retired railway employees.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to date the Canadian National Railways board of directors, who are trustees of the pension fund, have authorized all changes to the pension plan. The plan is administered by a pension board consisting of an equal number of labour and management representatives with whom the company discusses proposed changes in the plan and from whom the company receives proposals for changes.
On the pension issue, I am informed that this year, for the first time, the unions included pension demands in their notices to bargain. The major demand is that the present plan, which provides a pension of li per cent of the average of the best five years' earnings per year of service, be raised to a 2 per cent pension. CNR management and union representatives have agreed, subject to the conclusion of an over-all agreement, to adjust the present pension plan from the 1J per cent formula to a 2 per cent formula back to 1956.
