subtopic: GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATION-INCREASE IN DEPARTMENTS AND BUILDINGS IN OTTAWA-FUTURE POLICY
GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATION-INCREASE IN DEPARTMENTS AND BUILDINGS IN OTTAWA-FUTURE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 8 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) what, if any, are the limits to government growth in Ottawa. That question was sparked by news that the government had bought the Metropolitan Life Insurance building and the Orme building for $15,450,000 and intends to buy more property on Wellington Street for expansion of government departments. The Prime Minister answered by deflecting the question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube).
On February 22 I asked the Minister of Public Works how the huge government spending program in Ottawa
March 29, 1973

could be reconciled with "an effort to develop government services throughout western Canada." The minister seemed to treat the question lightly by pointing out that "obviously there are more government services in the capital of the country than elsewhere." However, he added that he agreed with me that "there could be some redistribution of power." It is redistribution of power in a physical and intellectual sense that this country urgently needs.
When I asked these questions, an Ottawa journalist wrote that I was "knifing" the city of my boyhood and forecast that when I rose tonight it would be to make an "anti-Ottawa" speech. This speech, Mr. Speaker, is not anti-Ottawa but pro-Canada. The unlimited growth of the federal bureaucracy in Ottawa is a reflection of the superman philosophy that characterizes this government. With every passing day as a Member of Parliament in Ottawa, I become more convinced that the federal government is too big, too dominant, too expensive and imposes itself too much upon people's lives.
Will this bureaucracy ever be limited? Obviously, it will not this year, Mr. Speaker, for the Department of Public Works is rushing along a spending program for Ottawa that exceeds the total amount of public works spending in the four western provinces and the two northern territories combined. The 1973-74 estimates show that the department is working on 22 major projects in Ottawa at a cost of $26.3 million. In the entire west and north, the department is spending $25.7 million on new projects. Similarly, the full spending budget for all operations in the city of Ottawa is $97.4 million, while the full spending budget in the west and north is $73.1 million.
On March 19, 1973, appearing before the miscellaneous estimates committee, the Minister of Public Works justified this enormous spending program in Ottawa because the number of civil servants is increasing by 5 or 6 per cent a year, "and you do have to find space to house them." Then he went on to make the incredible statement that because Canada is prosperous "it is normal that the capital of our nation does increase; we are all in favour of that."
Well, Mr. Speaker, I am not in favour of this never ending escalation of civil servants who need ever more office space, and neither are millions of Canadians who do not live in the capital city, however majestic its scenery especially at tulip time. No wonder the federal government's budget has tripled in ten years and that the 1973-74 fiscal year will see a 17 per cent increase in expenditure. Ten years ago there were 197,998 civil servants, and today there are 277,336. Ten years ago the government payroll for civil servants was $852,731,321, and now-hold on to your hat, Mr. Speaker-it is $2,284,666,035. As if the number of permanent civil servants is not high enough, the total projected costs for 1973-74 for professional and outside services are $600 million. This is an increase of $60 million over last year.
So I return to my first and basic question. What are the limits to government growth in Ottawa? Obviously the Minister of Public Works will go on putting up buildings until the philosophy of government changes. We must rank as the most overgoverned nation on earth. The Economic Council of Canada has warned that the federal
Adjournment Debate
government is chiefly to blame for the fact that government at all levels occupies 36 per cent of the gross national product. Why do we need 5,000 civil servants in Statistics Canada, many of whom spend their days writing harassing letters to business people in my constituency demanding all sorts of answers to questions? Why do we need 9,000 people in National Health and Welfare? Why do we need the small army working in unemployment insurance offices? Somebody has to blow the whistle and yell, "Stop. The taxpayers have had enough." We are not going to finance this bureaucracy any more, especially when, with all this expertise, the government cannot solve the unemployment and inflation crises.
Let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, that western Canada feels what I have just expressed, and it is time the government listened to the west. The federal government is now preparing, in conjunction with the four western provinces, a conference on western economic opportunities. I hope this conference is a vehicle to move the country ahead positively and that the federal government will listen to our ideas on taxation, energy, agriculture, distribution of powers, transportation and the development of manufacturing. As a starting point for the conference, I commend to all its participants the excellent series of articles entitled "What Does the West Want?" now appearing in the Edmonton Journal. I want it to be a success, and so do other western MPs. Consider, then, how shocked I was to learn that Members of Parliament will have no part to play, even as observers, in this historic conference.
I want to warn the government that if it holds this conference behind closed doors and excluses western Members of Parliament, this will be the ultimate sham in ignoring that noble phrase of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), "participatory democracy." The conference will doubtless import many civil servants from Ottawa, some of whom know nothing of conditions in the modern west, to advise it. The very people who know a lot about the west, who have been elected and have the confidence of westerners-the MPs-will be excluded.
In the case of Alberta, which elected 19 Conservative MPs, which means that there is no MP in Alberta with a direct link to the government, this situation will be ludicrous. In effect, the government will be penalizing Albertans for voting Conservative by keeping out of the conference any federally-elected Alberta voice. This is hardly any way to start a western conference of rediscovery and reconciliation. The west wants to be heard. We want the federal bureaucracy stabilized and decentralized. The Department of Public Works spending program shows that, however beautiful the words, we have a long way to go in this fight.

If the hon. member were accurate, his remarks might be forgiven. But he is not. His assertion that the federal public service has increased by 10 per cent over the past year is simply not founded on fact. The latest figures released from Statistics Canada on this subject are for the third quarter of 1972. On September 30 of that year, total federal government employment, which includes employment in all departments, departmental corporations, agency corporations, proprietary corporations and other agencies and corporations, stood at 417,487 persons. This figure compares with 402,079 persons at the end of September, 1971, an increase of 3.8 per cent in that period, far below the 10 per cent figure suggested.
The hon. member also spoke of growth in the public service over what he referred to as a period of "several years". Over the period 1963 to 1971, the latter being the latest year for which data are available for the full year, the record shows that total federal government employment has increased at an average annual rate of just under 2 per cent. This rate of growth compares favourably with the average growth of total employment in the provincial public service of 5.9 per cent, and the 2.7 per cent rate of growth in the total number of employed persons in Canada over the same period.
In terms of manpower strength with regard to the measure of full-time, continuing employment used by the Treasury Board to control manpower authorization in the public service, the average annual increase over the period 1963-72 has been 1.72 per cent, considerably less than the 2.71 per cent average annual rate of increase in total employment in Canada.

THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-SUGGESTED INTRODUCTION OF GUARANTEED ANNUAL INCOME TO ALLEVIATE UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to complete my question of February 21 which appears on page 1520 of Hansard and which reads:
Since the minister recognized that it is impossible for him to find a satisfactory solution to the problems of unemployment and that, consequently, the rate of unemployment, already heartbreaking, particularly in the case of the young, will go up unavoidedly, could the minister tell us if he considered setting up a guaranteed annual income as a possible solution to that unfortunate situation?
Mr. Speaker, the necessity for a guaranteed and vital minimum income for all Canadians 18 years old and over is quite obvious. Present programs fail to stimulate the flow of products towards consumers.
In the past, capitalists asserted that salary increases were to be compensated by higher productivity.
According to a Financial Post article which was printed in La Presse of last March 6, productivity has increased by 28 per cent since 1966 but manpower in the manufacturing industries has expanded by only 6.5 per cent.
The financial weekly comments particularly upon the decision of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to revise completely before 1974 the fiscal provisions which allow for the fast write-off of capital expenditures, and all the other tax incentives designed to stimulate investments in the manufacturing sector.
Now, even if the accelerated write-off helps reduce costs, promotes modernization and benefits the economy, such a practice seldom creates new jobs directly and promptly.
If capital cost allowances must continue as part of financing enterprises, the revision ordered by the Minister of Finance could show that at best they serve to prevent losses in jobs.
For, taking into account the huge and universal impact of technological advance on the manufacturing industry, employment in manufacturing plants does not expand significantly in any industrialized countries. What does increase is competition on the markets for disposal of a rapidly rising production.
Therefore, the core of the matter is not so much a race between countries to increase employment as an endeavour aimed at maintaining employment at a stable level.
According to us members of the Social Credit Party, the logical solution, a solution which is gaining currency among a large proportion of our people, would be to grant a compensated discount and a guaranteed vital minimum income to each citizen of this country, which would allow production to reach the consumer, the consumer being the first aim of any production.
Moreover, the guaranteed minimum income would result in levelling regional disparities.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) never said of course that he considered it was impossible for him to solve the unemployment problem. On the contrary, he has always claimed that creating jobs is and has always been his first preoccupation. Besides, statistics confirm that the picture has improved; for instance, more than 350,000 jobs have been created from February 1972 to February 1973. The last estimates of the Minister of Finance give eloquent evidence of his firm will to boost the Canadian economy. In the budget highlights we notice to this effect the following words:
The rate of expansion this year should provide jobs fast enough to bring about a significant reduction in unemployment. A year from now 300,000 more Canadians should be holding jobs.
Expansionist measures have been adopted to create this favourable economic environment. These measures include notably an increase in the basic exemption for all taxpayers from $1,500 to $1,600 as of January 1, 1973; an increase in the exemption for married couples from $2,850 to $4,000 as of January 1, 1973, a reduction of 5 per cent in the basic federal tax, the maximum reduction being $500 and the minimum reduction $100, also as of January 1, 1973.
Moreover, the federal government has set a series of additional employment programs, including the Local Initiatives Program, on the Job Training Program and Winter Capital Projects Fund Program, etc. which are particularly directed to those aspects of the unemployment problem which react very little to the traditional tax mechanisms.

As to the guaranteed income, in the Speech from the Throne, the government clearly enunciated its position on the matter of amending reconsideration of the social security system in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote a few excerpts of that speech, which, in my opinion, are quite relevant.
In the area of social policy, the Government considers that Canada's total social security system-including both federal and provincial elements-must be reconsidered and reorganized, and made more sensitive to the needs of people in different parts of the country.
The Government intends that this reorganization should be based on five principles which, taken together, comprise a statement of the Government's commitment in respect of social security.
First, the social security system must assure to people who cannot work, the aged, the blind and disabled, a compassionate and equitable guaranteed annual income.
Second, the social security system as it applies to people who can work must contain incentives to work and a greater emphasis on the need to get people who are on social aid back to work.
Third, a fair and just relationship must be maintained between the incomes of people who are working at or near the minimum wage, the guaranteed incomes assured to people who cannot work, and the allowances paid to those who can work but are unemployed.
Fourth, it must be recognized that Provinces may wish to have the structures of social security vary in accordance with the social needs, income standards and the cost of living in different communities.
